title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

title: The impact of prophylactic azithromycin on the developing preterm gut microbiome and resistome
abstract: Early-life antibiotic exposure can profoundly impact the developing preterm gut microbiome and resistome, with short- and long-term consequences for health. In a large multi-center ( = 28) study of 693 preterm infants, we investigated the effects of 10 d of prophylactic intravenous azithromycin on the gut microbiome and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). The AZithromycin ThErapy for Chronic Lung Disease of Prematurity (AZTEC) study was a double blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of preterm infants (born < 30 weeks of gestation), treated from birth for 10 d with either intravenous azithromycin or placebo, and sampled longitudinally for 21 d or discharge. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, antibiotic susceptibility testing, and quantitative PCR, we show azithromycin reduced microbial diversity and the relative abundance of health-associatedand increased relative abundances of pathobiontsand. This early azithromycin treatment increased the number of macrolide-resistant genes, including the presence of(C), which persisted for the duration of the study. Probiotic use (at individual unit discretion) increased alpha diversity andrelative abundance, but did not fully mitigate the effects of azithromycin receipt. Combined azithromycin and probiotics further increased the enrichment ofand total ARGs, including(C). These findings highlight the impacts of antibiotic and probiotic use, both important in balancing infection control issues and microbiome disruption and antimicrobial resistance.

title: Modulation of the gut microbiome and resistome by antibiotic use, but not by subsequent 2'-fucosyllactose intake, in adults with overweight or obesity
abstract: Antibiotics are widely used to treat bacterial infections, yet overuse and misuse causes disruption of the gut microbiome and spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Presence of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) could be a determinant of the response to antibiotics. Supplementation with prebiotics may limit the detrimental antibiotic-induced effects on the microbiome, but whether this results in changes in the gut resistome is unclear. This study investigated the impact of eight-week 2'-fucosyllactose (2'-FL) supplementation after seven-day vancomycin use in 18 adults with overweight/obesity, a subset from a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized intervention. Whole-metagenome shotgun sequencing was used to characterize the gut microbiome and resistome at baseline, after vancomycin use and after supplementation. Seven-day vancomycin use disrupted microbial richness and diversity ( < 0.001) and changed microbial composition. No improvements in microbial recovery were detected after eight week 2'-FL supplementation compared to placebo. Resistome richness and diversity were not affected by vancomycin use, although the presence of specific ARGs changed. No differential impact of 2'-FL supplementation on resistome richness, diversity and composition was detected. While vancomycin use disrupted the gut microbiome and affected the resistome, the detectable effects of 2'-FL supplementation were limited. Future research should investigate antibiotic- and prebiotic-induced changes in the gut resistome in more detail.

title: Effects on health and antioxidant status of oral supplementation of hazelnut skin extract in dairy calves with neonatal diarrhea: a randomized clinical trial in hospitalized patients
abstract: Neonatal calf diarrhea (NCD) is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in calves. Growing concern about antimicrobial resistance has spurred interest in phytotherapeutic alternatives, particularly polyphenol-rich extracts. Hazelnut skin (HS), a by-product of the confectionery sector, is a sustainable and underutilized source of polyphenols; however, its therapeutic efficacy in calves with NCD remains insufficiently investigated. This randomized, parallel-group clinical trial evaluated the effects of oral HS extract supplementation as an adjunct to standard medical therapy in hospitalized dairy calves with NCD. Sixty female Holstein calves were randomly allocated to a control group (CTRL; = 30) or a treatment group (HS; = 30) receiving 10 g/day of HS extract with milk for 5 days. All calves received standardized clinical management, including fluid therapy and antimicrobial administration. Clinical parameters, milk intake, body weight, hospitalization outcomes, sepsis scores, and blood oxidative stress biomarkers were monitored. No significant differences were detected between groups for clinical recovery, fecal score, hydration status, milk intake, weight gain, hospitalization duration, mortality, or oxidative stress markers. Clinical improvement over time was evident in both groups and was attributable to standard therapy. In conclusion, short-term oral supplementation with HS extract did not confer additional clinical or antioxidant benefits when added to conventional treatment in calves with NCD.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

abstract: Mastitis is a multifactorial disease with major consequences for production, animal welfare, and public health, yet it remains less studied in goats than in cows. Moreover, reports of antimicrobial resistance among bacteria isolated from mastitic goats are scarce. In Ethiopia, treatment decisions for mastitis largely rely on empirical clinical experience rather than routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing. To address this gap, a cross-sectional study was conducted from November to December 2024 in Waghimra, Amhara, Ethiopia, to identify the major bacterial causes of mastitis and to evaluate their antimicrobial susceptibility patterns. Bacterial isolation, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing followed standard protocols, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 17 and WHONET software. The overall goat-level mastitis prevalence was 24.69% (98/397), comprising 2.52% (10/397) clinical and 22.28% (88/395) subclinical mastitis.spp. (47/129; 36.43%) was the predominant isolate, followed by(12/129; 9.30%) andspp. (3/129; 2.33%). Allisolates were resistant to ampicillin (37/37; 100%) and showed considerable resistance to tetracycline (16/37; 43.24%), but remained highly susceptible to kanamycin (36/37; 97.30%), chloramphenicol, and gentamicin (35/37; 94.59% each).andspp. were highly susceptible to most antimicrobials tested, except ampicillin. Multidrug resistance was detected in 13.46% (7 out of 52) of isolates, occurring exclusively amongspp. Subclinical mastitis, mainly caused byspp., was highly prevalent in the study area, showing complete ampicillin resistance and considerable tetracycline resistance. Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Antibiotic Stewardship, Resistance, and Mortality in Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococcus: A Quasi-Experimental Study of Linezolid Restrictions
abstract: Antibiotic restriction policies are intended to curb resistance, but their effects on resistance, timely treatment, and patient outcomes remain uncertain. We evaluated linezolid restrictions and whether vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) screening identifies patients most likely to benefit. We conducted a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences study using electronic health record data from 521,493 admissions at 2 academic medical centers from 2008 through 2019. Hospital 1 introduced a formal prior-authorization pager system in 2011 and stricter linezolid-specific criteria with enhanced post-prescription review in 2014; Hospital 2 served as a control. Outcomes included linezolid use, linezolid-resistant Enterococcus isolates, in-hospital mortality overall and by VRE status, and stewardship request behavior. Linezolid was used in 2.3% of admissions; 1.2% of Enterococcus isolates were linezolid resistant. Restriction policies were associated with a 27% reduction in linezolid use (-0.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -1.1 to -0.7; P < .001) and a 41% reduction in resistance (-1.0 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -1.6 to -0.4; P = .003). Overall mortality did not increase, but mortality among VRE-screen-positive patients increased by 4.7 percentage points (95% confidence interval, 1.9 to 7.5; P < .001), with larger increases among those with bacteremia or sepsis. Approval rates declined first, followed by fewer linezolid requests. Restriction policies can reduce antibiotic use and resistance but may benefit from screening-informed safeguards to preserve timely treatment for high-risk patients.

title: Integrative multi-omics reveals CUL4B as a modulator of macrophage pyroptosis and innate defense against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: (SA) causes a broad range of invasive human diseases, increasingly complicated by antibiotic resistance. Macrophages (MΦ) play a central role in innate immunity, yet key aspects of their interaction with SA remain incompletely understood because of the pathogen's diverse immune evasion strategies. Using multi-omics and systems-level analytics, we identified the E3 ubiquitin ligase cullin 4B (CUL4B) as a host factor that modulates MΦ responses to SA infection. CRISPR-mediated deletion of CUL4B in human THP-1 MΦ enhanced intracellular bacterial killing, reduced cell death, decreased caspase-1 activation, and lowered interleukin-1β production, consistent with altered inflammasome signaling. In a murine methicillin-resistant SA (MRSA) pneumonia model, CUL4B deficiency improved pulmonary bacterial clearance, reduced bacteremia, and decreased inflammatory tissue injury. Whole-lung and serum proteomics further revealed increased antimicrobial protein abundance and reduced markers of inflammatory damage. Together, these findings identify CUL4B as a regulator of MΦ inflammatory responses during MRSA infection and suggest a potential host-directed pathway that could be leveraged to improve outcomes against this major pathogen.

title: Research on the spillover risk of antibiotic resistance gene from the gut microbiome of wild animal: A case study of the golden snub-nosed monkey
abstract: Wild animals are "reservoirs" of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), and the interface of rivers between wild animals and humans is an ideal environment for spreading ARGs. In order to explore the risk of ARGs from wild animals to the human ecosystem through rivers, metagenomic sequencing was used to obtain the microbiome in the gut of golden snub-nosed monkeys () and in the rivers. We performed collinearity analysis between the high-risk ARGs (Rank I ARGs) from golden snub-nosed monkeys and the metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from river samples to assess the potential of river microorganisms to acquire Rank I ARGs. The number of collinear events between Rank I ARGs and MAGs in the WHD group (rivers within the disturbed monkey habitat) was five times higher than that in the WCK (rivers within the undisturbed monkey habitat) group. This implies a significant spillover risk of ARGs from wild animals to the human ecosystem via river interfaces, a risk that is further intensified by human disturbances. This research complemented the content that evaluated the spillover risk of ARGs from wild animals to humans.

title: Network-based characterization of latent co-testing patterns in antimicrobial susceptibility testing
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance depends on antimicrobial susceptibility testing, yet antibiotic panels vary by pathogen cohort, specimen, year, ward, and care setting. We term these empirically reconstructed testing architectures shadow antibiograms: structures that shape which susceptibility results enter surveillance datasets and which resistance relationships can be observed. We analyzed approximately 13 million bacterial isolates from Germany's National Antibiotic Resistance Surveillance system (2019-2023) across six WHO BPPL-aligned operational cohorts. Co-testing networks were constructed using Jaccard, Dice, cosine, and phi-coefficient similarity, evaluated with Fisher's exact tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, and partitioned with multi-resolution Louvain community detection. Networks contained three to four dominant co-testing communities; false discovery rate (FDR) retention ranged from 89 to 100% across cohorts and specimen types. Jaccard provided the best balance of coherence, stability, antimicrobial-class alignment, interpretability, and edge retention. This work provides one of the first national-scale empirical characterizations of shadow antibiogram structure, supporting diagnostic stewardship and bias-aware AMR surveillance interpretation.

title: A Retrospective Benchmark of Quantitative Antimicrobial Peptide Activity Prediction Tools
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are critical candidates for addressing the global antibiotic resistance crisis. AI-driven quantitative models capable of directly predicting peptide antimicrobial activity, specifically minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), are gaining scientific prominence by providing precise guidance for the rational design of AMPs. To assess their real-world, out-of-the-box performance, we conducted a retrospective benchmark of 10 publicly released quantitative AMP prediction tools spanning classical machine learning and contemporary deep learning approaches. Using an external dataset and reconstructed native datasets, we evaluated absolute MIC regression, retrospective reproducibility, directional prediction patterns, ranking capability, and virtual-screening enrichment. Most released tools exhibited poor absolute MIC regression and limited transferability to the external benchmark, while selected tools retained useful relative-ranking and enrichment capabilities. Retrospective evaluation further revealed marked differences in implementation-level reproducibility among the released tools. Error-stratified analyses identified systematic associations between prediction errors and peptide residue composition, together with a general compression of the predicted activity range. Collectively, these findings characterize the practical performance boundaries of currently accessible quantitative AMP prediction tools and support their use primarily as early-stage screening filters rather than precise substitutes for experimental MIC measurements.

title: Spatial Variation of Antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli along Bagmati River, Kathmandu Valley
abstract: Antimicrobial resistant Escherichia coli has been reported in Bagmati river of Kathmandu Valley; however, studies on its spatial distribution are lacking, despite being essential for effective water management. Therefore, this cross-sectional study was conducted to determine the spatial distribution of antibiotic-resistant E. coli along Bagmati river from March-September 2025. This work was conducted at Department of Microbiology Tri-Chandra Multiple Campus. Water samples collected in duplicate from fifteen sites of Bagmati river were processed for most probable number count and isolation of E.coli. BOD and DO were calculated by Winkler's titrimetric method. Antibiotic susceptibility test was done by disk diffusion technique. Chi square test, correlation assessment, cluster and factor analysis were conducted. The coliform count, E. coli isolates, Biochemical oxygen demand and dissolved oxygen levels ranged from 5-26,500 MPN/100 mL, 0-42, 1.2-418.75 mg/L, and 8.05-0.15 mg/L, respectively, from Baghdwar to Chobar. No E. coli isolates were recovered from Site 1. Cluster analysis based on these variables classified river into four distinct segments, with Sites 1 and 15 forming separate clusters. Significant differences were observed in antibiotic resistance pattern of E. coli isolates across the sampling sites. Factor analysis further grouped the river sites into five clusters, indicating spatial variation in antimicrobial resistant E. coli along the river continuum. Conventional water quality indicators are insufficient to capture spatial complexity of river health. Integrating fecal contamination and antibiotic resistance patterns provides a more comprehensive assessment of pollution hotspots, supporting targeted management strategies under Nepal's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0.

title: Priorities and opportunities for strengthening hygiene and One Health alignment in research, policy and practice
abstract: Hygiene plays a critical yet under-recognized role in addressing One Health (OH) challenges, including zoonotic disease prevention, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) control, food safety and protection of ecosystem health. Likewise, hygiene research and interventionsgenerally lack an OH perspective, resulting in siloed efforts that inadequately address the human-animal-environment interface. We convened three sessions at global conferences well attended by health professionals working in hygiene or OH. Participants identified gaps and opportunities for hygiene-OH alignment across research, policy and practice at community, national, regional and global levels. An evidence gap identified was research on hygiene approaches to protect ecosystems in programs otherwise focused upon human or animal health. Methodological priorities included harmonizing tools and protocols for pathogen detection, fecal contamination measurement and hygiene behavior assessment; strengthening cross-sectoral data sharing; and developing integrated study designs. Intervention opportunities included engaging local stakeholders, balancing infrastructure and behavior change, adapting existing programs for cross-sectoral relevance and broadening evaluation to include animal and environmental outcomes. Implementation priorities included localized program design and decision-making, regional cooperation for cross-border threats and leveraging surveillance and preparedness infrastructure. Policy priorities included reducing institutional fragmentation, harmonizing standards, and strengthening the roles of hygiene and OH within existing regulatory frameworks. From our synthesis, we present cross-cutting recommendations for strengthening hygiene and OH alignment. Aligning hygiene and OH offers a pathway to more comprehensive and upstream prevention of disease and AMR, supporting coordinated, system-level management of health risks across human, animal and environmental domains and building resilience to emerging health threats.

title: Emergence of ESBL-Producing Escherichia coli in Shrimp Aquaculture, Kerala, India
abstract: The present study evaluated 63 shrimp aquaculture farm sites in the Thrissur and Alappuzha districts of Kerala State, India. A total of 206 samples were analyzed, and 50 extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli strains were identified with antibiotic susceptibility testing (AST) profiles. All the strains were multidrug-resistant (MDR), with multiple antibiotic resistance (MAR) indices ranging from 0.32 to 0.64. PCR detection revealed a high prevalence of ESBL genes, bla(86%), bla(58%), bla(50%), DHA (58%) and bla(48%). Quinolone and fluoroquinolone genes are aac(6')-Ib-cr (100%), qnrS (78%), OqxA (52%), OqxB (18%) and qnrB (8%). Non-ESBL genes included tetA+tetB (98%, 2%), sul1+sul2 (90%, 76%) and cmlA (48%). Plasmid replicon typing showed that IncFIB and IncN (96%), IncI1 (92%), IncFIC (78%) and IncFIA (56%) as predominant plasmid types. Phylogrouping revealed the presence of pathogenic lineages B2 (40%) and D (14%), whereas phylogroups E (86%) and C (82%) were more prevalent. Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) demonstrated high genetic heterogeneity among the strains, indicating non-clonal dissemination across farms. These findings indicate a surge in ESBL-producing E. coli exhibiting elevated resistance mechanisms, posing a significant public health threat. This underscores the urgent need for coordinated cross-sectoral interventions to mitigate AMR risks, curb the dissemination of resistance genes, and safeguard aquatic ecosystems and public health.

title: When does environmental antimicrobial resistance become a health risk?
abstract: Environmental antimicrobial resistance (AMR) only constitutes a meaningful risk when resistant bacteria overcome key ecological and transmission barriers to reach, persist in, and colonize susceptible hosts. By linking exposure, evolution, transmission, and ecology, our framework provides a realistic basis for assessing AMR risks across One Health compartments.

title: Antimicrobial resistance trends and lineage distribution among invasive pneumococcal disease isolates pre- and post-pneumococcal conjugate vaccine introduction, South Africa
abstract: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV) have reduced antimicrobial-resistant invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) globally. We evaluated trends in antimicrobial-resistant IPD and pneumococcal lineages before and after PCV13 introduction in South Africa. We analysed national, laboratory-based IPD surveillance reported cases (2005-2020) and compared the incidence of resistant-IPD pre- and post-PCV introduction. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed for six antibiotics, and penicillin-multidrug resistance (penicillin-MDR) was defined as penicillin nonsusceptibility plus resistance to ≥2 additional antibiotic classes. Whole-genome sequencing was used to determine serotypes, sequence types, global pneumococcal sequence clusters (GPSC), and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants. Following PCV introduction, overall IPD and AMR IPD incidence declined substantially. Penicillin-cotrimoxazole nonsusceptible and penicillin-MDR IPD incidence decreased from 5.6 to 0.8 per 100,000 population (percentage decrease -86.5%, confidence intervals [CI] -90.5% to -81.4%) and 5.5 to 0.4 (-93.0%, -95.7% to -89.1%), respectively, in children <5 years, with smaller but significant reductions in the ≥5 years old. Despite these declines, residual PCV13 serotypes, particularly 19A and 19F, continued to contribute notably to penicillin-cotrimoxazole nonsusceptible and penicillin-MDR IPD, respectively, after PCV13 introduction. Non-vaccine serotypes (10A, 15A, 15B/C, 16F, 23B, and 35B) increasingly contributed to resistant IPD in the post-PCV13 era through the expansion of both vaccine-type and non-vaccine-type GPSC lineages. PCVs substantially reduced AMR IPD in South Africa, but persistent PCV13 serotypes and expanding resistant non-vaccine-type lineages highlight the potential benefit of higher-valency PCVs, including PCV20.

title: Eleven-year surveillance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections and antimicrobial resistance trends in a Portuguese tertiary hospital, 2014 - 2024: Trends and insights into novel agents
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a frequent hospital-associated pathogen, often causing severe infections with limited treatment options due to increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains. This study evaluated its prevalence and resistance patterns in a large tertiary hospital. A retrospective observational study analysed all P. aeruginosa clinical isolates collected over 11 years (2014-2024) from inpatients and outpatients. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing included carbapenems, cephalosporins, piperacillin-tazobactam, aztreonam, aminoglycosides, ciprofloxacin, fosfomycin, colistin, ceftolozane-tazobactam and ceftazidime-avibactam. A total of 22883 P. aeruginosa isolates were analysed, representing 16802 episodes from 9978 patients. Mean patient age was 60.9 ±24.7 years, with male predominance. The prevalence of P. aeruginosa among hospitalized patients was 3.0%. Overall, 11.9% of isolates were MDR, 3.3% XDR and 84.8% non-MDR, with MDR and XDR rates increasing over time (p<0.05). A difficult-to-treat phenotype was present in 4.2%. Resistance to at least one carbapenem was observed in 19.0% of isolates, and to ciprofloxacin in 20.3%. Susceptibility to piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, ceftazidime, and amikacin remained above 80%. Most isolates non-susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftazidime remained susceptible to amikacin, supporting amikacin-containing combination regimens in high-risk settings. Colistin resistance remained below 1%. Among MDR isolates, susceptibility to ceftazidime-avibactam decreased between 2017 and 2024 (100.0% to 83.7%, p<0.05), whereas ceftolozane-tazobactam susceptibility fluctuated over time (83.1% to 88.2%, p<0.05). These findings reveal a shifting resistance landscape and underscore the need for sustained surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship, and updated empirical treatment strategies, while highlighting a critical gap in contemporary epidemiological data.

title: High prevalence of hypervirulent Staphylococcus aureus CC22-t309 in Pediatric Osteomyelitis and Septic Arthritis in China
abstract: This study aimed to elucidate the molecular epidemiology, virulence factors, and antimicrobial resistance profiles of Staphylococcus aureus isolated from children with osteomyelitis and septic arthritis (OM-SA) in China. A total of 68 S. aureus isolates were collected from pediatric patients with OM-SA in Shanghai, China, with 100 strains from children with other infections serving as controls. We performed a systematic analysis on all strains by integrating clinical metadata, whole-genome sequencing, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Among S. aureus isolates from OM-SA cases, CC22-t309 was the dominant clone (32.3%), followed by CC59-t437 (17.6%). The prevalence of CC22-t309 in OM-SA was much higher than that in the control (32.3% vs. 8.0%, p<0.001). OM-SA patients with CC22-t309 infection presented much higher inflammatory markers than those infected with other clones (p<0.05). Notably, CC22-t309 from OM-SA exhibited higher carriage of virulence factors, including Panton-Valentine leukocidin (pvl, 100%), collagen adhesin (cna, 86.4%), and fibronectin-binding proteins (fnbA/B, 77.3%), compared with other clones (pvl, 0∼66.7%; cna, 0∼13.8%; fnbA/B, 0∼24.1%; p < 0.05). Within CC22-t309 clone, the carriage of pvl, fnbB and fnbA showed no difference between OM-SA and control group (pvl: 100% vs. 87.5%; fnbB: 77.3% vs. 85.7%; fnbA: 77.3% vs. 37.5%; p >0.05). However, the prevalence of cna in OM-SA was significantly higher than that in the control group (86.4% vs. 37.5%, p = 0.015). Furthermore, CC22-t309 isolates displayed a multidrug-resistant phenotype against β-lactams, macrolides, and lincosamides. We identify the hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant CC22-t309 as a high-risk S. aureus lineage associated with pediatric OM-SA.

title: Implementation of rapid pan-microbial metagenomics in paediatric intensive care: a single-centre, prospective, observational study
abstract: Few clinical metagenomics studies have reported rapid results with associated clinical impact or described deployment of protocols beyond centres in which they were developed. We aimed to assess the feasibility and clinical impact of implementing a previously validated rapid pan-microbial respiratory metagenomic service in paediatric intensive care, reporting protocol modifications, feasibility, diagnostic performance, clinical impact, and staff perspectives. This single-centre, prospective, observational study was carried out at a general paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) and a cardiac paediatric ICU in Great Ormond Street Hospital (London, UK) between Nov 4, 2024, and Feb 28, 2025. Respiratory samples were obtained from patients selected by intensive care staff based on clinical suspicion of lower respiratory tract infection, with no exclusion criteria. Samples were analysed by a well-established published metagenomic workflow that simultaneously detects bacteria, fungi, and DNA and RNA viruses and provides same-day preliminary results and next-day final results; separate aliquots were sent for concurrent culture and PCR testing. Clinical impact (change in antimicrobials, diagnosis, or infection control) was evaluated through electronic health record review. Clinical staff were surveyed for their feedback via an anonymous online semistructured questionnaire. 177 samples from 122 patients (median age 3·4 months [IQR 1·2-36·0]; 54% male) were tested. 174 (98%) samples passed quality control. Sensitivity at 16-h sequencing was 89% (95% CI 80-95) for bacteria, 100% (70-100) for fungi, and 87% (76-93) for viruses, with specificities greater than or equal to 99% across all kingdoms. 42 (24%) of 174 samples analysed by metagenomics yielded 50 organisms that were not detected by routine diagnostics, all of which were confirmed by orthogonal PCR testing. Clinical impact was observed in 51 (29%) of 174 samples, comprising changes in antimicrobial therapy in 46 (26%) samples. Of these 46 samples, 15 (33%) resulted in cessation of antibiotics, ten (22%) in initiation of antibiotics, six (13%) in a change of antibiotic therapy, and 15 (33%) provided confidence to continue an empirical antibiotic choice. Of the 33 ICU staff members surveyed, 23 (72%) reported a positive view of metagenomics, none reported negative views, and 22 (67%) perceived additional benefits over routine testing. This clinical pilot of rapid respiratory metagenomics in paediatric intensive care showed high specificity and good sensitivity. Protocols developed for an adult population were adapted to a paediatric population, including adaptations for polymicrobial upper respiratory tract samples, which are more common in children. However, increased sensitivity and antimicrobial resistance prediction will be required for broader clinical implementation. Although changes in patient management were observed, particularly for antimicrobial stewardship, delineating the true contribution of metagenomic results offered by this study is difficult. Multicentre studies over multiple winter seasons, with control arms and predefined selection of patients and sample types, are needed to assess the impact on patient outcomes and cost-effectiveness. NHS Respiratory Metagenomics Network (NHS England).

title: Antimicrobial Resistance and Molecular Epidemiology of Enterococcus Species Isolated at the University Hospitals of Sfax, Tunisia
abstract: Enterococci are major causes of both community-acquired and healthcare-associated infections. The rapid global dissemination of multidrug-resistant clones poses a major challenge to clinical management and infection control. The aim for the present study was to investigate the prevalence, antimicrobial resistance patterns, virulence genes, and molecular epidemiology of Enterococcus species isolated from clinical specimens in university hospitals of Sfax, Tunisia. A descriptive, hospital-based, cross-sectional surveillance study was conducted between March 2020 and February 2021. It included all Enterococcus strains isolated in the Microbiology Department of Habib Bourguiba University Hospital. Enterococcus isolates were tested for antimicrobial susceptibility in accordance with European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing guidelines. Polymerase chain reaction assays were performed to detect resistance genes (vanA, vanB, ermA, ermB, ermC, msrA, mefE, vga, vat, vgb), virulence genes (gelatinase [gelE], aggregation substance, enterococcal surface protein [esp], cytolysin, hyaluronidase), and the IS16 marker associated with the clonal complex 17 (CC17) lineage. A total of 231 Enterococcus isolates were recovered, including Enterococcus faecalis (62.3%) and Enterococcus faecium (34.2%). All E. faecalis isolates were susceptible to ampicillin, vancomycin, and linezolid; all E. faecium isolates were resistant to ampicillin, and 7.6% exhibited vanA-mediated glycopeptide resistance. The ermB gene was the predominant macrolide resistance determinant. Among E. faecium, esp (74.7%) was the most prevalent virulence gene, whereas E. faecalis mainly harbored gelE (78.5%). The IS16 element, characteristic of CC17 clones, was detected in 86.1% of E. faecium isolates. The present study highlights the emergence of multidrug-resistant E. faecium strains with molecular features suggestive of CC17 affiliation in hospital settings in Sfax, Tunisia, underscoring the urgent need for stronger infection control and antimicrobial stewardship programs.

title: Effects of substrate moisture content on physiological development, performance, and gut microbiome of black soldier fly larvae during swine waste treatment
abstract: Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) composting is a sustainable approach for treating swine waste. BSFL's performance depends on its digestive enzyme activity, which is shaped and enhanced by the gut microbiome. Moisture content influences gut microbiome composition and function; however, it is often overlooked, and its role remains poorly understood. We evaluated the effects of three moisture levels (65%, 75%, and 85%) on the larval gut microbiome, digestive enzyme activity, larval growth, protein content, and contaminant removal. Microbial communities in larval guts and substrates were characterized using 16S rRNA sequencing and multivariate analyses. Larvae reared at 65% moisture had the highest protein content (40.8% DM) and achieved significantly greater reductions in total organic carbon (85.4%), total nitrogen (47.9%), and total phosphorus (47.7%) than those reared at higher moisture levels. However, protease activity was highest at 75% moisture and alpha-amylase activity was highest at 85% moisture. Linear discriminant analysis effect size identified a more functionally enriched gut microbiome at 65% moisture, characterized by taxa associated with organic matter degradation, including Bacillaceae, Paenibacillaceae, and Caryophanaceae, and genera such as Paenibacillus, Peribacillus, and Stenotrophomonas, whereas higher moisture levels favored anaerobic and fermentative taxa. Spearman correlation analysis further identified associations between specific bacterial genera and enzyme activities, including a strong positive association between Enterococcus (enriched at 85% moisture) and alpha-amylase activity (ρ = 0.90). This study contributes to optimizing BSFL-based waste management and highlights the need for microbial enhancement strategies and research on antimicrobial resistance.

title: From passive carriers to selective filters: how microplastic aging shapes antibiotic resistance gene abundance
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are widely recognized as vectors for antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). However, pristine MPs are virtually nonexistent in nature. While environmental aging fundamentally alters MPs physicochemical properties, current studies report highly contradictory findings on how aging impacts ARG proliferation-ranging from synergistic enrichment to oxidative suppression-thereby precluding accurate ecological risk assessments. To resolve this conflict, we conducted a global meta-analysis of 701 independent observations. Aging significantly increased both absolute and relative ARG abundance (mean lnRR = 0.67 and 0.61, respectively), shifting MPs from passive carriers toward selective habitats. Critically, ARG abundance displayed non-linear temporal trajectories inferred from cross-study comparisons: absolute ARG abundance peaked at approximately 15 days of aging MPs, whereas relative ARG abundance showed a U-shaped pattern with a minimum at approximately 37.5 days. We propose a "boom-and-bust" conceptual model, in which an initial non-selective biomass surge is followed by late-stage, multi-stressor filtering; this model integrates our meta-analytic patterns with previously reported mechanisms and represents a hypothesis for direct experimental testing. Resistance mechanisms further diverged: efflux-pump genes peaked at mid-term aging on biodegradable polymers, while target-modification genes and mobile genetic elements remained enriched on high-surface-area recalcitrant plastics. Together, these findings suggest that aged MPs act as selective filters shaping the plastisphere resistome, and that aging state, temporal dynamics, and matrix-specific hotspots merit integration into antimicrobial resistance surveillance frameworks.

title: Microbial Culture Profiles Following Fetal Surgery Versus Spontaneous Preterm Prelabor Rupture of Membranes in Multifetal Gestations
abstract: To assess microbial culture profiles and antibiotic resistance patterns in pregnancies complicated by preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPROM) following fetal surgery compared with spontaneous PPROM without fetal surgery. This retrospective cross-sectional study included women with multiple pregnancies and PPROMs < 34 weeks who underwent fetal surgery between September 2018 and January 2024. The study group comprised those who had undergone fetoscopic laser surgery (FLS) or selective fetal reduction (SFR). Endocervical swab and urine cultures were obtained upon PPROM, and placental, uterine and neonatal blood cultures were collected at delivery. A control group included women with multiple pregnancies and PPROMs < 34 weeks without fetal surgery. Cases with other fetal surgeries, terminations of the pregnancy, or delivery prior to 23 weeks were excluded. Among 126 fetal surgeries, 39 (30.9%) developed PPROM; 32 met inclusion criteria. Compared to controls (n = 31), the fetal surgery group had higher rates of positive cultures (42.7% vs. 13.9% of site-level cultures, p < 0.01), and of ampicillin/macrolide resistance (18.8% vs. 4.3%, p < 0.01). There tended to be more positive placental cultures (43.8% vs. 25.8%, p = 0.47) in the fetal surgery group. No early-onset neonatal sepsis occurred in the fetal surgery group but one in the control group. PPROM following fetal surgery was characterized by a distinct bacterial profile and greater ampicillin/macrolide resistance than spontaneous PPROM. These exploratory findings warrant prospective confirmation before informing changes to clinical practice.

title: Non-Targeted LC-Q-Orbitrap HRMS Screening of Veterinary Drugs, Pesticides, and Emerging Contaminants in Animal-Derived Foods and Honey
abstract: Veterinary drug residues, pesticides, and chemical contaminants in animal-derived foods pose public health risks, including antimicrobial resistance development and consumer exposure to banned or withdrawn substances. Conventional targeted methods are inherently limited to predefined compounds and may overlook emerging or unexpected contaminants. Many developing countries still lack comprehensive multi-residue surveillance across diverse food matrices, highlighting the need for analytical frameworks adaptable to regulatory laboratories. To evaluate an LC-Q-Orbitrap HRMS framework combining reference-standard-assisted confirmation with non-targeted screening for the detection and identification of veterinary drug residues, pesticides, and chemical contaminants across multiple animal-derived food matrices. A streamlined extraction protocol coupled with liquid chromatography-quadrupole-Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry was applied to 450 retail samples collected in Egypt, covering nine matrices (bovine liver, kidney, meat, heart, raw bovine milk, chicken breast, chicken eggs, honey, and Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus)). Confirmation used 36 certified reference standards; non-targeted screening used Compound Discoverer™ with spectral database matching and in silico fragmentation prediction. Nine compounds were confirmed at Level 1 (confirmed structure via reference standard match) according to the Schymanski identification confidence framework, accounting for 74 detection events, most frequently oxytetracycline (18 detections) and trimethoprim (17 detections). Non-targeted screening revealed 45 additional compounds identified at Level 2a (probable structure based on library spectrum match), including antimicrobials, β-agonists, pesticides, and pharmaceuticals. Phenacetin and tapentadol were each detected in 48 samples, and fenobucarb in 30% of milk samples. Liver and honey showed the greatest diversity of detected compounds. HRMS-based non-targeted screening extends analytical coverage beyond predefined reference-standard panels in multi-matrix food surveillance. LC-Q-Orbitrap HRMS detected 54 compounds across nine animal-derived food matrices-nine Level 1 confirmations and 45 Level 2a probable structures-extending chemical surveillance beyond reference-standard panels.

title: Etiological characteristics and infection-related biomarkers in patients with severe community-acquired pneumonia in the emergency department: A retrospective cohort study
abstract: Severe community-acquired pneumonia (SCAP) remains a leading cause of infectious disease mortality worldwide. Timely identification of causative pathogens and appropriate antimicrobial therapy are critical determinants of patient outcomes. This retrospective cohort study investigated the etiological features of SCAP and their relationship with infection-related biomarkers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), D-dimer (D-D), white blood cell count (WBC), and neutrophil percentage (NEUT), in an emergency department setting. A total of 146 patients with SCAP admitted to Tianjin Medical University General Hospital between March 2018 and March 2019 were included. Pathogen identification was performed through sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cultures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was conducted using the Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion method. A total of 154 bacterial strains were isolated from 146 patients. Gram-negative bacteria predominated (145 strains, 94.2%), followed by Gram-positive bacteria (8 strains, 5.2%). The most frequently isolated pathogens were Klebsiella pneumoniae (25.3%), Acinetobacter baumannii (20.1%), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (13.6%). Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing strains were identified in 17 of 39 K. pneumoniae isolates (43.6%). High-risk clones of K. pneumoniae ST11, ST15, ST307, A. baumannii ST2, P. aeruginosa ST235 were detected in this study. Cefoperazone-sulbactam demonstrated low resistance rates in K. pneumoniae (7.7%), A. baumannii (9.7%), Enterobacter cloacae (8.3%), and P. aeruginosa (14.3%). Abnormal PCT levels were associated with higher proportions of K. pneumoniae and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia infections. Elevated CRP, D-D, WBC, and NEUT levels were more frequently observed in patients infected with K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii. Gram-negative bacteria, particularly K. pneumoniae and A. baumannii, are the predominant pathogens in SCAP. Infection-related biomarkers, especially PCT, show promise in predicting specific etiologies and may guide empirical antimicrobial selection.

title: Activity of a three-phage combination against Mycobacterium tuberculosis in disease-relevant conditions
abstract: Phage therapy offers promise to combat antimicrobial resistance, including drug-resistant tuberculosis. Understanding phage activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in granuloma-like microenvironments that induce non-replicating states, characterized by hypoxia and acidity, is essential. To evaluate a phage combination against Mtb under hypoxic, acidic (pH 5.5), and stationary-phase conditions in vitro. Mtb H37Rv cultures were grown to exponential phase for time-kill studies (106 colony forming units (CFU)/mL) under normal, hypoxic, and acidic conditions. Hypoxia was generated using sealed containers with gas sachets. Stationary-phase cultures were grown for 14-21 days and used undiluted. Treatments included control media, single phages (Fred313cpm-1Δ33, FionnbharthΔ45Δ47and Muddy HRM N0157-2), phage combination (multiplicity of infection 10:1), and rifampicin or isoniazid (0.1 µg/mL each). Phage titers (measured using M. smegmatis overlays) and bacterial counts (CFU on Middlebrook 7H11) were assessed at repeated time-points. Longitudinal phage-bacteria dynamics mixed-effects modelling and simulation was performed. In actively growing cultures, phage levels rose by day 7, followed by sustained reductions in Mtb counts over 31 days. Phages prevented regrowth seen with antibiotics alone. Acidic conditions variably affected individual phage stability and activity. Under hypoxic and stationary conditions, phage titers remained stable, but no reduction in Mtb was observed. Model-based predictions adequately captured phage-mycobacterial interactions with and without rifampicin. Productive lytic activity was not observed in assays with non-replicating mycobacteria. Established models can support future experimental designs. This study provides mechanistic insights driving progress in the field of phage therapy development.

title: Beyond Principlism: A Cosmopolitan and Care Ethics Approach to One Digital Health
abstract: This article examines the limitations of principlism in addressing the ethical challenges posed by One Digital Health. While principlism remains influential in bioethics, digital health, and global health policy, we argue that it is insufficient to capture the relational, data infrastructural, and multispecies dynamics shaping the threats to One Health. Using antimicrobial resistance as a paradigmatic case, we show that One Digital Health governance is shaped not only by distributive ethical concerns but also by structural asymmetries in data visibility, digital infrastructure, and epistemic inclusion across human, animal, and environmental domains. These asymmetries reveal a key limitation of principlism: although it articulates abstract commitments to justice and equity, it lacks the conceptual and operational resources to explain how inequalities are produced and reproduced in digital systems. To address this gap, we propose an integrated framework that combines the ethics of care, cosmopolitanism, and a FAIRER-based account of data governance. Ethics of care foregrounds situated vulnerability and relational interdependence; cosmopolitanism extends moral responsibility across global and multispecies scales; and FAIRER operationalizes these commitments within digital infrastructures and data systems. The antimicrobial resistance case study shows that this approach provides a more comprehensive account of One Digital Health governance by linking lived practices, global responsibilities, and data infrastructures. We conclude that addressing One Health threats through digital transformation requires moving beyond principle-based reasoning toward relational frameworks that integrate global commitments with contextual sensitivity.

title: Comparative genomic analysis of Agrobacterium salinitolerans provides insights into genetic diversity and pathogenic potential
abstract: Agrobacterium spp. are widespread plant pathogens, particularly associated with crown gall disease, and their genomic features and ecological adaptations underlie complex plant-microbe interactions. Agrobacterium salinitolerans, a relatively understudied member of this genus, exhibits distinct genomic traits that may contribute to its pathogenicity and environmental persistence, yet its genetic architecture and adaptive mechanisms remain poorly characterized. In this study, we conducted a comparative genomic analysis of A. salinitolerans strain YN6, isolated from crown gall tissue of Rosa spp., alongside 14 publicly available A. salinitolerans genomes. Pan-genome analysis, supported by average nucleotide identity (ANI) and digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH), revealed an open pan-genome structure indicative of high genetic diversity. This diversity is primarily driven by mobile genetic elements (MGEs) and horizontal gene transfer (HGT), while most core and accessory genes are maintained under purifying selection. We identified numerous virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes linked to macromolecular secretion systems, underscoring the strain's genomic features associated with plant-pathogenic interactions. Additionally, a rich repertoire of carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) genes was detected, suggesting broad metabolic versatility and enhanced survival across diverse ecological niches. This study provides a comprehensive genomic characterization of A. salinitolerans, revealing its high genetic plasticity, evolutionary dynamics, and multifaceted ecological adaptations. The findings highlight the species genetic repertoire linked to host colonization and environmental survival strategies, laying a critical foundation for future functional genomic investigations.

title: Comparative genomic characterization of publicly available human- and food-associated Aeromonas genomes from diverse countries
abstract: Aeromonas spp. are emerging and neglected human pathogens widely distributed in nature. Despite their medical importance, the genomic characteristics of this genus remain incompletely understood.
