This study screened A. hydrophila (n = 63), A. veronii (n = 236), A. dhakensis (n = 78), and A. salmonicida (n = 13) genomes from strains isolated from human and food sources across 19 countries over a 42-year period for antimicrobial resistance, stress, and virulence genes, as well as plasmid replicons. Their genetic relatedness was assessed by searching single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) clusters, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), core-genome MLST (cgMLST), and fragmented-genome analyses. A total of 123 genes encoding resistance to 13 antimicrobial classes and 16 genes associated with heavy-metal tolerance and resistance to heat and disinfectants were observed. Six plasmid replicons were detected in 19 genomes. A total of 245 virulence genes associated with adhesion, secretion systems, and toxins were identified. All phylogenetic analyses suggested high intraspecies diversity, regardless of isolation country, year, or source. In conclusion, the high diversity and frequency of clinically important antimicrobial resistance and virulence genes carried by genetically diverse strains of clinically and environmentally relevant Aeromonas species reinforce the potential hazard of infections caused by these pathogens and the need for more effective surveillance by public health authorities.

title: Progressing From Association to Causation: Examining Prior Antibiotic Exposure and Antimicrobial Resistance Across Three US Health Systems Using Causal Machine Learning
abstract: Antibiotic exposure is hypothesized to drive antimicrobial resistance, but confounding by indication has limited causal inference from observational data. We estimated the effect of prior exposure on subsequent same-class nonsusceptibility across 7 antibiotic classes and 3 US health systems using a causal-inference framework. We analyzed 1 165 151 culture episodes from Mass General Brigham (MGB), Stanford Health Care, and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC; via MIMIC-IV). The causal effect of 90-day prior exposure on same-class resistance was estimated by double machine learning, adjusting for more than 35 confounders per site, including prior same-class resistant isolates, infecting-organism group, and calendar period. Robustness was assessed via inverse probability weighting, E-values, exposure-window and dose-response sensitivity, and negative-control pairs. Rates of microbiologically inactive empiric therapy were compared by prior same-class exposure. Prior fluoroquinolone exposure was associated with increased nonsusceptibility by 11.9 and 12.6 percentage points at the primary sites (MGB, Stanford) and 8.6 points in validation (BIDMC) (all P < .001). Positive associations occurred for all 7 classes at all sites (sulfonamides indeterminate at Stanford), strongest at 30 days and attenuating through 365 days. Among patients with prior fluoroquinolone exposure receiving empiric fluoroquinolones for bloodstream infection, therapy was inactive in 50%-71% of episodes versus 27%-37% without prior exposure. Across classes, 3309 inactive empiric prescriptions were associated with prior same-class exposure. Median E-value was 2.5. Prior antibiotic exposure was consistently associated with increased same-class nonsusceptibility across antibiotic classes and health systems, paralleling higher rates of microbiologically inactive empiric therapy. These findings support prospective evaluation of antibiotic-history-informed empiric prescribing.

title: Prior Antibiotic Exposure and Subsequent Resistance in the Individual Patient: How Close Are We to the Bedside?
Draft genome sequence analysis of a multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli sequence type 3602 isolated from an equine placentitis lesion in Kentucky, USA
abstract: We report the draft genome sequence of a multidrug-resistantisolate recovered from an equine placentitis lesion associated with late-term abortion. This genome expands available genomic resources for equine-associatedand supports investigation of antimicrobial resistance in equine reproductive disease.

title: A PhoP-regulated type II secretion system drives bacterial competition in Serratia marcescens
abstract: is an enteric bacterium that can act as an opportunistic pathogen, with increasing incidence in clinical settings. This is largely due to its ability to express a broad repertoire of virulence factors and acquire antibiotic resistance mechanisms. Consequently,has been designated by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a research priority for the development of alternative antimicrobial strategies. In this study, we identify a previously unrecognized role of the type II secretion system (T2SS) in mediating bacterial competition in the clinical strainRM66262. Phylogenomic analysis reveals that the T2SS is conserved among clinical isolates but absent from most environmental strains, suggesting it confers a selective advantage in host-associated or highly competitive environments. Functional assays demonstrate that the T2SS contributes to both inter- and intraspecies antagonism and acts in concert with the contact-dependent type VI secretion system (T6SS), with both systems contributing additively to bacterial killing through distinct mechanisms. We further show that T2SS expression is positively regulated by the PhoP/PhoQ two-component system through direct binding to its promoter region and is induced in response to competitive cues such as attack by. Altogether, our findings expand the functional scope of the T2SS beyond classical extracellular virulence, establishing it as a PhoP-regulated system involved in bacterial competition and a promising target for novel anti-virulence strategies. This work uncovers a previously uncharacterized role for the type II secretion system (T2SS) in, demonstrating its involvement in both inter- and intraspecies bacterial competition. The finding that the T2SS is conserved among clinical isolates but largely absent in environmental strains suggests that this system confers a selective advantage in host-associated or high-competition settings. Furthermore, we show that T2SS expression is regulated by the PhoP/PhoQ system and induced by interbacterial contact, underscoring its role in adaptive antagonistic responses. By expanding the known functional scope of the T2SS, this study provides new insights into the ecological strategies of opportunistic pathogens and highlights a promising target for anti-virulence therapeutic development.

title: Electron transport chain: a crucial target of luteolin in combating Trueperella pyogenes
abstract: is an opportunistic pathogen capable of causing infections in both domestic and wild animals. Furthermore, the dissemination of resistance genes has resulted in varying degrees of antimicrobial resistance amongisolates. Therefore, it is necessary to develop new anti-.drugs to address its increasing resistance. Luteolin, a natural flavonoid, has been found to exhibit good antibacterial activity againstin our previous research. This study aims to utilize high-throughput proteomics technology to identify potential novel targets and illuminate the action mechanism of luteolin. Our results indicated that luteolin could target electron transport chain complexes I, II, and V to inhibit the oxidative phosphorylation of. Besides, luteolin could inhibit the enzyme activities involved in glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid cycle, which eventually leads to a decrease in reduced hydrogen supplied to the electron transport chain and reduces the content of intracellular adenosine triphosphate. Based on the high-throughput proteomic analysis and multiple experimental results, the inhibition of electron transport chain complexes appears to be a significant mechanism by which luteolin exerts its antibacterial effect against. Overall, this study provides a new insight into the anti-.mechanism of luteolin and offers new targets to develop anti-.drugs. is an opportunistic pathogen that can cause suppurative infections in multiple animals. Its existing resistance may bring challenges to anti-infection therapy. As a promising natural antibacterial agent, luteolin shows potent activity against this bacterium. This study revealed that luteolin disrupts bacterial energy metabolism by targeting electron transport chain complexes, thereby reducing intracellular adenosine triphosphate content. Our findings expanded the new antibacterial mechanism of luteolin and identified novel targets. This work provides valuable references for developing novel drugs against drug-resistant bacterial infections by targeting the electron transport chain.

title: PanRes: A database of latent and acquired antimicrobial resistance allowing 3D-based protein homology search
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance databases are central to genomic surveillance, but resistance determinants remain distributed across resources with different scopes, structures, and annotations. We developed PanRes, a curated resistance database of 11 717 genes integrating acquired and latent determinants of antibiotic, biocide, and metal resistance within a unified ontology. We predicted representative protein structures and clustered them by structural similarity, grouping proteins into 505 high-confidence structurally conserved clusters coherent despite sequence divergence. Their structure-guided alignments were used to build Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) for remote homology search. In seven wastewater metagenomes from five European cities, PanRes 3D-based HMMs expanded detection beyond what was possible with BLAST, with 35.3% of retained hits identified only by the HMMs and generally showing greater divergence from known proteins. For beta-lactamases, several proteins retained beta-lactamase-like folds and catalytic geometry despite weak sequence similarity. PanRes is available through an interactive web platform (https://panres.rambio.dk/), a structure-informed resource for exploring the whole resistome. The database, HMM profiles, and ontology are available at Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.22876216). Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: Insights into the recent advancements of cephalosporins and their nanoformulations in antibacterial applications
abstract: Cephalosporins are extensively utilized β-lactam antibiotics for the treatment of respiratory, skin, soft tissue, urinary tract, and systemic bacterial infections. However, their extensive and inappropriate use has augmented antimicrobial resistance, reducing their clinical effectiveness. This review recapitulates the physicochemical properties, antibacterial mechanisms, and the challenges of the development of resistance to cephalosporins. Bacteria can develop resistance via pathways, including production of β-lactamase enzymes, mutations in penicillin-binding proteins, efflux pumps, and reduced aqueous-filled protein channels in the outer membrane, which restrict cephalosporin entry. The literature survey was conducted in PubMed, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect using relevant terms. The current review elucidates the role of nanoparticles in overcoming antibiotic resistance to cephalosporins. Lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, and hybrid nanocarriers can help avoid antibiotic resistance by disrupting bacterial membrane defenses; limiting drug resistance mechanisms, such as blocking efflux pumps and inactivating β-lactamases; reducing biofilm formation; providing targeted drug delivery; and enhancing solubility. The nanoformulations of first- to fourth-generation cephalosporins demonstrate improved pharmacokinetic performance and therapeutic outcomes against multidrug-resistant pathogens, whereas studies on fifth-generation cephalosporins remain limited. The primary challenges that hinder clinical translation of cephalosporin-based nanoformulations include β-lactam instability, formulation scalability, regulatory approval, low drug loading, and long-term safety.

title: The influence of antibiotic perturbation on methane oxidation from the perspective of cross-media coupling: Effects, mechanisms and prospects
abstract: Methane oxidation represents a vital biological sink for mitigating methane emissions and climate warming. However, the responses of methane oxidation to antibiotic exposure, together with the associated ecological consequences, remain insufficiently understood. This review synthesizes current evidence on the environmental consequences of antibiotic-induced perturbations to methane oxidation and the mechanisms underlying these effects across multiple scales and environmental compartments, including soils, freshwater sediments, estuarine wetlands, aquaculture sediments, and biofilms in constructed wetlands. Particular attention is given to aerobic methane oxidation and denitrifying anaerobic methane oxidation, with antibiotic effects evaluated at the molecular, physiological, microbial-community, and ecosystem levels. At the cellular level, antibiotics may interfere with particulate methane monooxygenase activity and induce reactive oxygen species-mediated oxidative stress, whereas dose- and exposure-duration-dependent effects may produce low-dose stimulation, high-dose inhibition, or other non-monotonic response patterns. At broader ecological scales, these direct effects are further modulated by antibiotic-induced changes in redox conditions, nitrogen and sulfur cycling, microbial community composition, microbial interaction networks, and antibiotic resistance gene enrichment; collectively, these changes reshape methane oxidation capacity. Available evidence therefore indicates strong environmental-compartment dependence, process specificity, and dose-time dependence in the response of methane oxidation to antibiotic exposure. By altering the balance between methane production and consumption, these perturbations may ultimately modify net methane fluxes and thereby generate additional feedbacks to climate warming. This review provides a mechanistic framework for understanding antibiotic-induced perturbations of methane oxidation, identifies priorities for future research, and supports the integration of methane-cycle responses into ecological risk assessment and environmental management across diverse environmental compartments.

title: Correction: Multidrug antibiotic resistance index and antimicrobial resistance patterns of Escherichia coli in intensive pig farms in Kenya
Bacterial strategies for surviving antibiotics during urinary tract infection: could uropathogenic Escherichia coli be persisters?
abstract: Treating bacterial infections, such as urinary tract infection (UTI), with antibiotics does not always resolve the infection and often results in subsequent re-infection. Treatment failure can be driven by bacterial mechanisms of resistance, tolerance or persistence, collectively known as the antibiotic non-response. Antibiotic resistance is well characterized across various bacterial species and implicated in poor clinical outcomes in various infection settings. In the instance of resistance, bacteria harbour genetic determinants to evade antibiotics and continue to grow during treatment. Notably, bacteria can escape antibiotic killing in the absence of resistance genes. In response to the environment, an entire bacterial population can slow its growth rate, becoming tolerant to bactericidal antibiotic exposure. Alternatively, a subpopulation of bacteria, known as persister cells, survive whereas the remainder of the population is eliminated by bactericidal antibiotics. Both mechanisms enable bacteria to survive treatment, with the capacity to regrow following cessation of antibiotic treatment. However, our understanding of tolerance and persistence in the context of UTI is limited. Thus, two bacterial phenotypes that might contribute to poor outcomes are overlooked both in the clinic and in research, which could add to the challenges of treatment failure and recurrent UTI.

title: Thermophilic pig manure compost as an additive for sewage sludge composting: humification efficiency and changes in heavy metals, antibiotics, and antibiotic resistance genes
abstract: Thermophilic livestock manure compost harbors microbes with vigorous metabolic activity, making it a promising natural inoculant for composting systems. However, there has been no documented application of thermophilic livestock manure compost as an additive in sewage sludge composting. The impacts of this strategy on shifts in heavy metal speciation and the removal of antibiotics and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) during sludge composting remain poorly understood. In this study, thermophilic pig manure compost materials (TM) were used as additives and incorporated into sewage sludge composting to evaluate its effects and underlying mechanisms on humification efficiency, heavy metal immobilization, and the removal of antibiotics and ARGs. Results indicate that TM significantly improved organic matter degradation rate, germination index, and humification index by 26.9%, 18.9%, and 35.8%, respectively, while reduced the composting maturation period by at least five days. TM significantly decreased both the concentrations and exchangeable fractions of Zn, Pb, As, and Ni in sludge compost, as well as their accumulation in corn seedlings (P < 0.05), by modulating key environmental factors (moisture content, carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and pH) and influencing the microbial community structure. TM facilitated the removal of tetracycline, sulfonamide, and quinolone antibiotics, and reduced the prevalence of ermA, ermF, sul1, sul2, tetM, and tetX by decreasing the abundance of ARGs-hosting microorganisms (e.g., Pseudomonas, Streptomyces, Flavobacterium, Bordetella, Escherichia, and Klebsiella) and mobile genetic elements (e.g., intl1, intI2, and Tn916/1545). These results offer a scientific basis for the resource recovery and utilization of sewage sludge.

title: Potential clinical actionability of metagenomic next-generation sequencing for antimicrobial stewardship for urinary tract infections: a retrospective, single-centre, BI-Biotia UTI cohort study
abstract: Culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) take 48-72 hours, leaving empirical therapy for urinary tract infections (UTIs) without resistance data. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) reports resistance within hours, but its potential clinical actionability for prescribing is underexplored. In a retrospective single-centre cohort (Bangkok tertiary hospital, 2018-2020), BIOTIA-DX results were compared with culture and AST in 251 culture-paired samples. Potential clinical actionability was assessed for 54 same-day empirical prescriptions and a post hoc ablation estimated what a rule-based policy would have prescribed under different information from mNGS. Twenty-two of 54 prescriptions (40·7%, 95% CI 28·7-54·0) were potentially actionable: treatment failure prevention 9 (16·7%) and de-escalation 13 (24·1%). Excluding blaEC and blaACT raised cephalosporin specificity from 25·6% to 78·9% with a small tradeoff in sensitivity. NPVs were at least 89·7% for carbapenems, cephalosporins, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, aminoglycosides and the fluoroquinolone classifier reached 100·0% PPV in Escherichia coli. Our refined resistance classification rules achieved a good tradeoff between the risk of ineffective antibiotics and the use of broad-spectrum carbapenem, compared with observed prescribing. In a high-resistance setting, a same-day mNGS report was potentially actionable for two in five empirical prescriptions, mainly through resistance calling. However, the findings rest on a small number of cases.

title: Genomic epidemiology reveals niche specialization and a virulence-resistance trade-off in ST23 and ST11 hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: The convergence of hypervirulence and carbapenem resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae poses a critical public health threat, yet the comparative genomic characteristics and adaptation patterns of dominant clones ST23 and ST11 in clinical settings remain unclear. This study aimed to characterize their divergent adaptive strategies. We performed whole-genome sequencing on 824 hvKP isolates derived from 2,193 clinical Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates collected at a National Regional Medical Center in Central China. Among these, ST23 (n=199) and ST11 (n=140) represented the two predominant sequence types and were compared regarding antimicrobial resistance profiles, resistance determinants, virulence determinants, plasmid replicon types, and phylogenetic relationships using comparative genomic, phylogenetic, and co-acquisition analyses. ST23-hvKP was primarily associated with surgical and medical departments, largely antibiotic-susceptible (MDR 33.7%, CR 1.0%), with near-complete virulence gene profiles (iuc 99.5%, iro 97.5%). Conversely, ST11-hvKP was predominantly ICU-associated and extensively drug-resistant (MDR 97.9%, CR 93.6%), characterized by frequent blacarriage (95.7%) and a highly prevalent IncFII(pHN7A8) replicon (98.6%), with blastrongly associated with IncFII(pHN7A8), but with an incomplete virulence profile (iro 0.7%). Resistance-hypervirulence convergence was markedly higher in ST11 (92.1%) than ST23 (9.5%). Plasmid ecology and co-acquisition analysis revealed a negative correlation between resistance-associated (IncFII/IncR) and virulence-associated (IncFIB(K)) replicons, suggesting that convergence in ST11 involves coexisting distinct plasmid systems rather than detectable plasmid fusion events. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated distinct clustering patterns between ST23 and ST11. ST23 retains a classic hypervirulent phenotype, whereas ST11 represents a hospital-adapted convergent clone characterized by a complex resistome, an incomplete canonical virulence repertoire, and separate plasmid systems. This niche-specialized resistance-virulence trade-off underscores the need for clone-tailored surveillance and management strategies.

title: AI strategies to combat antimicrobial resistance
Concentration-dependent effects of metal(loid) exposure on bacterial conjugative transfer: a meta-analysis and machine learning study
abstract: Metal(loid) contamination of aquatic and agricultural systems is a global concern, yet its impact on conjugative transfer of antibiotic resistance genes under environmentally relevant concentrations remains unquantified. We synthesized 556 effect sizes from 56 studies using three-level meta-analysis with machine learning. This approach identified concentration and metal type as the most important predictors. The U-shaped dose-response curve showed a positive association at low concentrations (<∼1 mg/L), the strongest negative association near 322.6 mg/L, and a weakening of the negative association above this point. This pattern was most pronounced for copper (82.7% decrease at high concentrations). Recipient genera, including Salmonella, Acinetobacter, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus showed substantially stronger positive associations than E. coli recipients. Reactive oxygen species increased across donor, mixed, and recipient bacteria (64.2 - 91.3%) and correlated with overall effects (rho = 0.417, P < 0.001), suggesting oxidative stress as a potential mechanistic pathway underlying the observed associations. Metal concentrations typical of natural waters and agricultural systems generally fall below approximately 1 mg/L, within the range associated with increased conjugation. This alignment extends to regulatory limits: even WHO guidelines for As, Cd, Pb, and Cr, and Chinese Class I standards for Cu and Zn, fall within this range, underscoring its regulatory relevance. These findings provide a quantitative framework for assessing ecological risks associated with metal-mediated ARG dissemination and offer a basis for refining pollution control strategies.

title: Genomic Surveillance-Guided Phage Repository Construction and Rational Cocktail Design for Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae
abstract: Given the treatment delays inherent in reactive phage matching, we aimed to develop a preparedness-oriented strategy linking genomic surveillance of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP)to targeted phage-resource development and rational cocktail design. We analysed >64,000K. pneumoniae genomes to characterize the geographical and temporal representation of KL types within the genomic dataset. Phages were isolated and prioritized according to host-range profiles, genomic nonredundancy, receptor-binding protein diversity and morphology. Quantitative inhibition profiling and principal component analysis guided the selection of candidate combinations targeting KL64 isolates, followed by in vitro, in vivo, and resistance analyses. A limited number of KL types were frequently represented among the analysed CRKP genomes and showed regional variation. From a nonredundant repository of 33 phages, 10 were selected to target 10 frequently represented KL types. In a KL64 clinical isolate panel, selected combinations broadened and prolonged bacterial suppression., The phage cocktail significantly prolonged survival in mice under lethal CRKP challenge and phage-resistant derivatives showed restored susceptibility to multiple antibiotics. This study presents a framework for using genomic data to prioritize phage-resource development and guide cocktail design for KL-defined CRKP groups.

title: Antimicrobial resistance and antibiotic therapy in patients with urinary tract infections and asymptomatic bacteriuria: A Peruvian perspective
abstract: Overdiagnosis and overtreatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and asymptomatic bacteriuria (AB) increase antimicrobial resistance. The aim of this study was to evaluate resistance patterns and antibiotic therapy in patients with UTIs and AB in Peru. Cross-sectional study based on 164 urine cultures and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. A total of 62 cases of AB and 102 of UTI were identified. Women (116, 70.7%) and older adults (60, 36.6%) predominated. A total of 4582 antibiotic prescriptions were recorded, with a therapeutic pattern in both UTI and AB centered on the use of meropenem (540, 21.3%) and (333, 16.3%), vancomycin (221, 8.7%) and (454, 22.2%), ceftriaxone (369, 14.5%) and (176, 8.6%) and ceftazidime (227, 8.9%) and (274, 3.4%), respectively. In general, antibiotic therapy was bactericidal in (87, 53.0%) cases, from the surveillance group in (98, 59.8%) cases, monotherapy in (112, 68.3%) cases, and in cycles of ≤7 days. UTI was associated with a higher burden of comorbidities, including chronic renal failure, hypertension, and diabetes. Fifteen bacterial species were isolated in both clinical entities, with a predominance of Gram-negative bacilli, mainly Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, both of which exhibited high resistance to cephalosporins, sulfonamides, and ampicillin/sulbactam. Among Gram-positive bacteria, Enterococcus faecalis and E. faecium showed resistance to erythromycin, tetracycline, and quinolones. The widespread use of antibiotics from the surveillance group and similar antibiotic therapy in AB and UTI, revealed a critical gap in the implementation of clinical guidelines and the urgent need to accurately differentiate between the two diagnoses to avoid overprescribing and help contain bacterial resistance.

title: Advances in the synthesis of bismuth-based heterojunction photocatalysts and visible light photodegradation of ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin in aqueous solutions: Degradation efficiency, degradation products, and their toxicity
abstract: Antibiotic pollution in water systems is a critical global challenge that worsens the global water scarcity crisis by contaminating vital freshwater reserves and creating dangerous antimicrobial resistance. Photocatalysis uses solar energy to power green catalytic treatments that clean antibiotic-contaminated water by breaking down persistent pharmaceuticals without using any harsh chemicals. Bismuth-based heterojunction photocatalysts leverage heterojunction engineering that drastically improves charge carrier separation and minimizes electron-hole recombination while enhancing redox potential for the destruction of environmental pollutants. In this article, we reviewed the removal of levofloxacin (LEV) and ciprofloxacin (CIP), the two most detected antibiotics in wastewater and aquatic environments globally, by various bismuth-based heterojunctions. Their photodegradation performance has been compiled and compared, and possible degradation routes, photodegradation mechanisms, and ecotoxicity of the degraded products are discussed. A true comparison of the degradation performance of CIP and LEV by various heterojunctions is difficult because various light sources, radiation intensity, pollutant concentration, and catalyst dose were used in various published studies. Of the heterojunctions so far developed, FeO/BiWOand BiO/(BiO)COshowed excellent CIP removal, and their photodegradation rate constants were 0.5571 and 0.476 min, respectively. Conversely, for the removal of LEV, BiWO/CuS and BiOCl/BiFeOprovided excellent photodegradation, and the rate constants were 0.2639 and 0.0934 min, respectively. Toxicity analyses show that many degradation intermediates of CIP and LEV are toxic and mutagenic if the photodegradation is incomplete. The development of low-cost photocatalytic drug removal technology based on bismuth-based heterojunctions holds significant potential to make drinking water safer for human and animal consumption.

title: Pneumococcal carriage and selected respiratory virus in children with clinical pneumonia in Salvador, Brazil during PCV10 era
abstract: In 2010, Brazil introduced the 10-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV10). Assessing pneumococcal carriage among children with clinical pneumonia in the context of a mature PCV10program can inform decisions about use of next-generation PCVs. We prospectively enrolled children aged 2-59 months meeting a standardized case definition for clinical pneumonia at two emergency care units in Salvador, Brazil. Nasopharyngeal specimens were tested for pneumococcus by culture and qPCR with serotyping by Quellung and/or PCR or qPCR; isolates underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST). Respiratory viruses were detected using qPCR, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) strains were genotyped. From March 2023 to March 2024, 170 children with clinical pneumonia were enrolled; 93.5% were up to date on pneumococcal vaccination. Pneumococcal carriage was detected in 62.7% (106/169 swabbed patients; 55 by culture and 51 by qPCR). Among the 106 pneumococcal carriers, the most prevalent serotypes were 6C (18.9%), 11A/D (9.4%), 19A (7.5%), 3 (6.6%), 19F (5.7%), 6A (5.0%), and 23B (4.7%). PCV10serotypes (19F, 4, 7F/A, 9V/A, 23F) were detected in 10.4% (11/106) of pneumococcal isolates, driven by serotype 19F (5.6%). The proportions of carriers with serotypes including in PNEUMOSIL, 13, 15, and 20 serotypes, were 21.7%, 29.2%, 30.2%, and 40.6%, respectively. Among 53 isolates with AST, more than 30.0% were resistant to macrolides and 35.8% were penicillin non-susceptible. RSV was detected in 20.6% (35/170) of cases, predominantly RSV-A (72.0%); 60.0% of RSV-positive cases were colonized with pneumococcus. More than a decade after PCV10introduction, and despite high vaccination coverage, PCV10serotypes remain detectable among pneumococci carried by children with pneumonia. Next-generation PCVs provide broader serotype coverage. Continued monitoring of the persistent circulation of vaccine serotypes remains important.

title: Innovative roadmaps for sustainable antimicrobial resistance interventions
abstract: Integrated strategies to combat antibiotic-resistant bacteria and fungi require innovative commercial models, new discovery platforms, standardized genomic surveillance, and streamlined clinical trials. Machine learning and other new technologies will accelerate the development of diagnostics and therapeutics (small molecules, antibodies, and vaccines) to combat antimicrobial resistance. Next-generation approaches should align societal impact with investment to ensure rapid global public health gains.

title: Rifampicin-resistant TB: An inflection point in antimicrobial resistance
abstract: Rifampicin-resistant TB should be integrated into the global AMR response through diagnostics, surveillance, and optimized treatment regimens.

title: In vitro assessment of the probiotic potential and safety of lactic acid bacteria for aquatic animal health
abstract: This study evaluated the in vitro probiotic-related properties and preliminary safety profiles of five lactic acid bacteria (LAB) strains for potential use in aquaculture: Limosilactobacillus reuteri ATCC 55730, Lentilactobacillus kefiri K107, Latilactobacillus sakei SN34, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum FI8595, and Streptococcus thermophilus BioSt64. Probiotic-related traits included antimicrobial activity against Lactococcus garvieae and Yersinia ruckeri, aggregation-related properties, and tolerance to fish bile and acidic conditions. Safety assessment included hemolytic and enzymatic activities and antibiotic susceptibility. Lmb. reuteri showed the strongest inhibition of L. garvieae (18.25 ± 1.06 mm), followed by S. thermophilus (9.85 ± 0.21 mm), whereas Ltb. sakei inhibited Y. ruckeri (9.00 ± 0.00 mm). All strains coaggregated with both pathogens and remained viable under the tested acidic and bile conditions. Lmb. reuteri and Lpb. plantarum showed high autoaggregation and cell surface hydrophobicity, which may indicate potential for intestinal adhesion, although this should be confirmed through direct adhesion assays. S. thermophilus showed the most favorable preliminary profile, combining antimicrobial activity, absence of detectable hemolysis, and susceptibility to most antibiotics under the conditions tested. Lmb. reuteri also showed promising probiotic-related properties, but its previously reported antimicrobial resistance determinants represent an important safety concern, while the β-hemolytic activity of Ltb. sakei precludes its selection without further assessment. Further controlled in vivo evaluation is required before any of these strains can be considered for use as aquaculture probiotics.

title: Design and optimization of naringenin-loaded organogels for topical management of bacterial infections
abstract: Bacterial skin infections are increasingly complicated by antimicrobial resistance, and naringenin, a citrus flavanone with membrane disrupting antibacterial activity, is limited in topical use by poor aqueous solubility and low dermal penetration. The present work was undertaken to develop and optimize naringenin loaded organogels for topical antibacterial application using a systematic quality by design approach. Naringenin loaded organogels were prepared by the hot emulsification technique and optimized through a 3full factorial design in which glyceryl monostearate (10 to 20% w/w) and Capryol™ PGMC (5 to 15% w/w) concentrations were varied. The formulations were characterized for gel strength, viscosity, spreadability, drug content, drug excipient compatibility by FTIR, in vitro drug release, release kinetics, antibacterial activity and accelerated stability. The pH values (6.12 to 6.42) were suitable for topical application and the drug content was high (96.8 to 99.1%). Gel strength (42.6 to 92.2 g) and viscosity (3842.6 to 9922.3 cps) increased with glyceryl monostearate concentration, whereas spreadability (16.5 to 29.6 g · cm/s) decreased. Response surface methodology identified MF5, containing 15% w/w glyceryl monostearate and 10% w/w Capryol™ PGMC, as the optimized formulation, with experimental values for gel strength (78.5 g), viscosity (6082.4 cps) and drug release at 12 h (89.74%) closely matching the predicted values (relative error below 2.5%). The optimized formulation followed zero order release kinetics (R = 0.9859) with a non Fickian diffusion mechanism (n = 0.79), retained antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, and remained stable under accelerated conditions for three months. Optimized naringenin loaded organogel exhibited favorable physiochemical properties with an sustained in-vitro drug release and antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus. The optimized formulation showed reduced antibacterial activity under the same experimental conditions when compared with the standard ciprofloxacin, and showed to release the antibiotic continuously from the organogel matrix. By using the factorial design approach, an optimized formulation having reproducible quality attributes and acceptable physicochemical stability after accelerated storage was achieved.

title: Real-World Use of Ceftazidime-Avibactam for Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Infections in Children: A 7-Year Cohort From a Latin American Referral Center
abstract: Pediatric data on ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ-AVI) for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) infections remain limited, particularly in Latin America, where KPC-producing organisms are endemic. We describe the clinical characteristics, microbiological profile, and outcomes of children with CRE infections treated with CAZ-AVI at a tertiary referral center in Colombia. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of children younger than 18 years with clinically significant CRE infections treated with CAZ-AVI between January 2018 and June 2025. Clinical, microbiological, treatment, and outcome data were collected. The primary outcome was clinical response at the end of therapy. Forty-three patients were included (median age, 11 years [IQR, 6-15]); 25 patients (58%) were immunocompromised, 29 (67%) required PICU admission, and 16 (37%) presented with septic shock. Klebsiella pneumoniae was the predominant pathogen (33 patients, 77%), and KPC was the most common carbapenemase detected (39 patients, 91%). Clinical improvement within 72 hours occurred in 40 patients (93%), with a median time to response of 2 days (IQR, 2-3). Overall, 40 patients (93%) achieved clinical cure. The estimated 30-day survival probability was 95.3% (95% CI, 88.8-100), recurrence occurred in 3 patients (7%), and no treatment-related adverse events were documented. In this real-world pediatric cohort from a KPC-endemic setting, CAZ-AVI was associated with favorable clinical outcomes and good tolerability. These findings support its role as an important therapeutic option for pediatric CRE infections and underscore the importance of mechanism-guided antimicrobial management.

title: bla(IMP-4)-associated imipenem susceptibility discordance in the Klebsiella pneumoniae complex: characterization and a phenotype-guided confirmatory workflow
abstract: Automated antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) may generate carbapenem minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) results differing from reference methods, complicating recognition of carbapenemase-producingcomplex isolates. We characterized carbapenem susceptibility discordance in a retrospective discovery cohort of 133 carbapenemase-producing isolates collected in Shenzhen (2004-2017) by comparing imipenem (IPM) and meropenem (MEM) MICs obtained by VITEK 2 and broth microdilution (BMD). Confirmed discordance was defined as repeat-confirmed raw MIC differences of ≥2 logdilutions. Features were assessed by whole-genome sequencing, mCIM/eCIM, and exploratory phenotypic assays. Cross-card reproducibility was assessed using an alternative VITEK 2 AST card. A separate retrospectively enriched cohort of 166isolates (2018-2024) was used to evaluate a phenotype-guided reflex-testing workflow. Twenty-nine isolates showed confirmed carbapenem AST discordance, including 28 with IPM discordance. Of these, 27 had raw VITEK 2 IPM MICs at least 2 log₂ dilutions higher than those obtained by BMD, whereas one was reported as resistant after system adjustment despite a low raw MIC. All discrepant isolates carriedas the sole detected carbapenemase gene, had relatively low carbapenem MICs by BMD, and were distributed across 14 sequence types. Cross-card retesting reproduced the direction of IPM elevation, although the magnitude varied. In a combined internal analysis set of 275 isolates, the phenotype-guided workflow identified unflagged ≥2 log₂ MIC discrepancies with 81.4% sensitivity (95% CI, 67.4%-90.3%) and 92.2% specificity (95% CI, 88.1%-95.0%). These findings define a repeat-confirmed-associated, IPM-predominant discordance between VITEK 2 and BMD and support phenotype-guided reflex-testing to identify unflagged MIC discrepancies and prioritize confirmatory testing in routine laboratories.IMPORTANCEClinical microbiology laboratories rely on automated systems to support antimicrobial susceptibility interpretation, but these systems may not always recognize method-dependent carbapenem susceptibility discordance. In this study, we show that a specific group of bacteria carrying thegene can produce potentially misleading carbapenem susceptibility results, particularly for imipenem, when tested by automated methods. These discrepancies may not be flagged by the instrument and could therefore be overlooked in routine practice. By combining routine laboratory data with genetic analysis and additional testing, we identify a recognizable pattern associated with these hidden discrepancies and examine a phenotype-guided confirmatory workflow to support their laboratory recognition. Our findings highlight the importance of targeted confirmatory testing and provide a framework for local validation of laboratory-actionable carbapenem susceptibility discrepancies, thereby supporting more reliable AST interpretation and antimicrobial resistance surveillance.

title: Draft genome sequences of five Escherichia coli strains with human pathogenic attributes from animal reservoirs in the United States
abstract: Both humans and animals harbor commensalor potentially pathogenic and drug-resistant strains that can cause severe infections. Here, we report draft genomes of five multidrug-resistantisolates from raccoon, mouse, and cattle in the USA, revealing antimicrobial resistance, virulence-associated genes, and plasmid-associated determinants relevant to One Health.

title: Invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella disease in the vaccine-development era: diagnostic blind spots, antimicrobial resistance, genomic transmission, and prevention
abstract: SUMMARYInvasive non-typhoidal(iNTS) disease is a severe bloodstream and focal invasive infection caused by non-typhoidal serovars of, especially. Typhimurium and. Enteritidis. Its clinical importance is disproportionate to its routine visibility because disease often presents as undifferentiated fever, sepsis, meningitis, severe anaemia-associated deterioration, recurrent bacteraemia, or focal infection, while definitive recognition depends on blood or other sterile-site microbiology. Global estimates indicate substantial mortality, but the true incidence remains uncertain because blood-culture access, prior antimicrobial exposure, specimen volume, and surveillance intensity vary widely. The vaccine-development era has intensified the need for a unified clinical microbiology framework. Prevention of invasive disease requires host-risk recognition, laboratory-confirmed endpoints, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, lineage-aware genomic surveillance, reservoir assessment, and post-introduction systems able to detect residual disease, breakthrough infection, non-target serovars, lineage shifts, and resistant invasive clones. This narrative review synthesizes the clinical, immunological, genomic, diagnostic, antimicrobial resistance, and vaccine era evidence relevant to iNTS control. Emphasis is placed on immune evasion, macrophage survival, T-cell dysfunction, immunosuppressed hosts, diagnostic blind spots, treatment under uncertainty, and the integration of laboratory systems with surveillance and prevention policy.

title: Non-Perturbative Bacterial Identification Directly From Solid Agar Plates Using Raman Micro-Spectroscopy and Machine Learning
abstract: Raman spectroscopy is a promising tool for microbial identification, yet its implementation in microbiology and clinical workflow is still restricted due to the accompanying additional preparation required to focus on microbial signals. Here, we demonstrate Raman-based bacterial identification directly from unopened, inverted agar plates, the same conditions used during incubation. Our approach enabled sensitive identification using two Escherichia coli variants, differing only in green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression, across diverse media and substrate material conditions, despite the interrogation path traversing 3-4 mm thick background material. We integrated traditional density functional theory (DFT)-based material computation with machine learning analysis, achieving over 97.7% classification accuracy, surpassing the performance of standard measurements from opened plates by 10.8% higher mean accuracy and 0.76% less variance. We further demonstrated Raman mapping-based colony identification via Raman peaks characteristic to GFPmut3 chromophore structure generated by DFT. Our approach is robust to changes in algorithms or substrate materials and promises real-time, non-perturbative monitoring of bacterial growth, biofilm formation, and antimicrobial resistance development.

title: Whole-Genome Sequencing-Based Characterization and Antimicrobial Resistance Analysis of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Isolated from Retail Meat Products
abstract: Shiga toxin-producing(STEC), a zoonotic foodborne pathogen, has become a critical global public health issue. This study investigates molecular traits and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) mechanisms of STEC strains derived from retail meat products sourced from domestic production in Liaocheng city, Shandong province, China, to inform health risk assessment. Using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), phenotypic AMR testing, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS), 38 STEC isolates were identified from 400 retail meat products, with an isolation rate of 9.5%. Significant differences in STEC isolation rates were detected among different meat types, and mutton exhibited a relatively high isolation rate of 26.09%. Genomic virulence analysis showed that there were higher proportions of single(58.33%) and dualgenotypes (33.33%) in mutton isolates than in beef (: 48.00%, dual: 12.00%), and only thegene was found in pork isolates. STEC isolates exhibited marked serotypic diversity, including O128ac:H2, O168:H7, O178:H7, O2:H25, and O6:H10. Multilocus sequence typing analysis revealed heterogeneous sequence type (ST) distributions among isolates, with,, andas dominant STs, suggesting diverse contamination sources. STEC isolates exhibited high phenotypic resistance to tetracycline (TET) (68.42%), which corresponded to the highest detection rate of the TET resistance geneat the genomic level. All isolates were susceptible to ertapenem, meropenem, ceftazidime, ceftazidime-avibactam, ciprofloxacin, and amikacin. Multidrug resistance (MDR) analysis indicated that 16 STEC isolates were MDR strains, with beef-derived isolates having relatively high MDR rates. This study verifies the occurrence of STEC in retail meat, highlighting prevalent AMR and substantial genetic heterogeneity among isolates. The findings underscore the necessity of systematic surveillance to limit STEC transmission along the meat supply chain and facilitate targeted food safety interventions.

Evaluation of the BioFire joint infection panel in Taiwan: Impact of regional non-target pathogens and joint type on its performance
abstract: The BIOFIRE® Joint Infection (BJI) panel, a rapid multiplex polymerase chain reaction assay, is used to diagnose joint infections. Here we used it to evaluate the clinical performance and impact of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) detection in Taiwan's unique microbial landscape. Adult patients with suspected septic arthritis or prosthetic joint infection were prospectively enrolled from four hospitals in southern Taiwan. Synovial fluid specimens were tested using a BJI panel and routine bacterial culturing. Performance was assessed by calculating the positive percent agreement and negative percent agreement (PPA and NPA, respectively). Eighty-six specimens (native joints, 56; prosthetic joints, 30) were analyzed. The overall PPA and NPA were 92.3% and 76.7%, respectively. Native joints showed higher concordance (PPA, 93.8%; NPA, 85.0%) than prosthetic joints (PPA, 90.0%; NPA, 60.0%). The BJI panel detected pathogens in 14 culture-negative cases, predominantly among patients who previously received antibiotics. Notably, the panel identified six methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus cases (three culture-negative) and one bla-positive E. coli detection. However, three culture-positive cases involving "off-panel" regional pathogens (Burkholderia pseudomallei, n = 2; Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, n = 1) were BJI-negative. Diagnostic concordance is better in native joints and correlated significantly with higher synovial leukocyte counts. Our evaluation revealed the BJI panel's ability to rapidly identify pathogens and profile AMR, with additional diagnostic yield particularly in culture-negative prosthetic joint infections and in patients with prior antibiotic exposure. However, its limited detection targets leave a diagnostic gap for regionally endemic pathogens such as Burkholderia pseudomallei and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, indicating the continued need for conventional culturing.

title: Assessment of antibiotic residues and microbiological safety in Lebanese dairy products: Akkawi cheese, yogurt, and labneh, collected across Lebanese dairy industries
abstract: Antibiotic residues in dairy products and the resulting antibiotic-resistant bacteria represent a major global public health concern. This study evaluated the microbiological safety of 400 dairy samples collected over two consecutive years (2022 and 2023) from 16 dairy residue industries across four governorates in Lebanon. In addition, antibiotic residues were screened from 126 dairy product samples randomly chosen out of the 400. An optimized multi-class method for the identification and quantification of 30 antibiotics was developed using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Results revealed that 48% of the analyzed samples were contaminated with at least one antibiotic residue, among which 33% showed co-occurrence of multiple antibiotic classes. Meanwhile, microbiological assessment of 400 dairy samples collected over 2 years from the same dairies revealed higher levels of contamination with total coliforms, Escherichia coli, and Staphylococcus aureus in Akkawi cheese samples collected during the first year (44%, 32%, and 15%, respectively) compared to those collected the second year (38.8%, 31%, and 0%). Moderate contamination levels were observed in Labneh (strained yogurt) samples collected during both seasons, with yeast (12%; 11%), molds (1.2%; 11%), total coliforms (6%; 11%), and Escherichia coli (3.7%; 11%). On the other hand, comparable levels of non-conformity were observed in yogurt samples across the two years, with contamination by yeast (7.5%; 6.2%), molds (3.75%; 6.2%), total coliforms (26%; 31.2%), E. coli (20%; 21%), and Staphylococcus aureus (1.25%; 0%). Escherichia coli isolates exhibited resistance to tetracycline while being 100% sensitive to ciprofloxacin and nalidixic acid. As for S. aureus isolates, they presented a high sensitivity to tetracyclines, doxycycline, and ciprofloxacin. These findings highlight the importance of implementing and maintaining good hygienic practices within dairy industries. Antimicrobial residues of oxytetracycline, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, sulfamethazine, and doxycycline were detected at levels below the maximum residue limits.

title: Substrate-dependent attenuation of antibiotic and metal resistance genes during acidogenic fermentation of titanium-flocculated sludge
abstract: Titanium-based coagulation enables efficient wastewater purification and sludge recovery, yet the fate of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and metal resistance genes (MRGs) during downstream sludge valorization remains insufficiently understood. Here, we investigated how food waste-derived substrates affected fermentation performance and ARGs/MRGs profiles during 7-day acidogenic co-fermentation of Ti-flocculated sludge. Substrate composition resulted in distinct fermentation characteristics and resistome responses. Compared with refractory fiber-rich substrates, readily hydrolysable starch promoted organic solubilization and acidogenesis, producing the highest soluble chemical oxygen demand and volatile fatty acid (VFA) concentrations. These fermentation characteristics were accompanied by the enrichment of polysaccharide-degrading and VFA-producing microorganisms, together with an increased representation of genes associated with glycolysis and carbohydrate-active enzymes. Concurrently, the relative abundance of mobile genetic element-associated genes decreased, accompanied by a reduction in total ARG abundance after fermentation. Protein-rich substrates showed distinct microbial and functional profiles, with higher relative representation of genes associated with proteolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and VFA-related metabolism. This treatment also markedly decreased the relative abundance of transposase-related genes, suggesting reduced mobility-associated potential of resistance genes. This study lays the foundation for evaluating resistance gene dynamics during co-fermentation of Ti-flocculated sludge.

title: Trends in Pseudomonas aeruginosa Resistance After a Four-Dimensional Antimicrobial Stewardship Intervention
abstract: This single-center retrospective study analyzed de-duplicated Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates collected at Huaian Municipal Infectious Diseases Hospital from 2023 to 2025. A total of 121 unique isolates were included, of which 83.5% were from sputum. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) was performed using an automated microbiology system, and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) results were interpreted according to CLSI M100, 33rd edition. In early 2024, a four-dimensional linkage-targeted antimicrobial stewardship intervention was implemented in the Respiratory and Tuberculosis Department (Resp-TB) (n = 97), comprising: (1) dynamic antimicrobial resistance surveillance with quarterly feedback; (2) risk-stratified antimicrobial prescribing based on local susceptibility data; (3) standardized specimen collection protocols; and (4) enhanced infection prevention and control measures. In the Resp-TB, the overall resistance rates were 74.19% in 2023, 81.63% in 2024, and 82.93% in 2025, with no significant reduction after the intervention (p ≈ 0.37). By 2025, resistance to tobramycin was 0/41 (0.00%), cefepime was 1/41 (2.44%), and piperacillin-tazobactam was 0/41 (0.00%); levofloxacin resistance reached 15/41 (36.59%). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole resistance remained high across the study period. These findings show persistent antimicrobial resistance in the Resp-TB after implementation of the intervention, while resistance to selected agents, including tobramycin, cefepime, and piperacillin-tazobactam, remained low in 2025.

title: BamA as a next-generation antibacterial target: mechanistic insights, inhibitor landscape, and rational drug design strategies
abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among Gram-negative pathogens has intensified the need for novel therapeutic strategies targeting previously underexploited bacterial systems. The β-barrel assembly machinery (BAM) complex, and particularly its central component BamA, has emerged as a highly promising antibacterial target due to its essential role in outer membrane protein (OMP) biogenesis and its accessibility at the bacterial surface. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of BamA structure, function, and mechanism, with emphasis on the dynamic lateral gate and β-augmentation processes that drive OMP folding and insertion. Recent advances in structural biology have enabled detailed characterization of BamA conformational states, offering critical insights into its druggability. We further present an integrated overview of the current BamA inhibitor landscape, including macrocyclic peptides, peptidomimetics, and small molecules, highlighting key structure-activity relationships (SAR) and binding modes. In addition, mechanisms of resistance, challenges associated with outer membrane (OM) permeability, and pharmacokinetic limitations are critically discussed. Particular attention is given to emerging design strategies that integrate conformational targeting, β-strand mimicry, and permeability optimization. Collectively, this review underscores the potential of BamA as a next-generation antibacterial target and outlines future directions for the development of effective therapeutics against multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria.

title: Coordination Reprogramming of Fe-Antibiotic Assemblies Enables Valence-Gated β-Lactam Reactivation
abstract: Reactivating legacy antibiotics offers a practical route to combat drug-resistant infections, but requires delivery systems that coordinate bacterial engagement with pathogen-triggered drug release. Here, we report DFC, a deferoxamine (DFO)-reprogrammed Fe-carbenicillin (Car) coordination nanoassembly that restores the activity of the legacy β-lactam antibiotic Car against MRSA. DFC was fabricated via DFO-mediated competitive coordination, transforming homogeneous Fe-Car networks into heterogeneous Car-Fe-DFO structures. Computational modeling and spectroscopic analyses showed stronger Fe-DFO affinity than Fe-Car binding, DFO-induced redistribution of the Fe-centered ligand environment, and sharply weakened Fe-ligand stability after Fe-to-Feconversion. This coordination reprogramming allowed DFC to remain assembled under nonreducing conditions but rapidly disassemble and release Car under reducing conditions or upon exposure to MRSA. DFC enhanced MRSA targeting, biofilm penetration, and intracellular Fe/Car-associated accumulation, while Fe-valence-triggered destabilization promoted Car release, disrupted iron homeostasis, amplified oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, and damaged the bacterial envelope. Collectively, these synergistic effects re‑established β-lactam susceptibility, conferred robust antibacterial and anti‑biofilm efficacy, and markedly promoted pathogen clearance as well as tissue repair, as evidenced in both infected wound and osteomyelitis models. This study establishes competitive coordination reprogramming as a chemical strategy for coupling bacterial iron metabolism with antibiotic liberation and resistance reversal.

title: High willingness to receive a vaccine for gonorrhoea prevention among gay, bisexual, queer, and other sexuality diverse men, and non-binary people in Australia
abstract: Gonorrhoea incidence and antimicrobial resistance are increasing among gay, bisexual, queer, and other sexuality diverse men, and non-binary (GBQ+) people. Observational studies suggested that 4CMenB vaccine (Bexsero®) may provide partial protection against gonorrhoea, but recent randomised trials found no clear evidence of protection. We analysed willingness to receive 4CMenB for gonorrhoea prevention in a 2025 Australian cross-sectional survey of GBQ+ individuals aged ≥16 years. Multivariable logistic regression examined associated factors. Among 2138 participants (median age 39 years), 89.2% were willing to be vaccinated. Willingness was lower among participants aged ≥30 (aOR = 0.46;95%CI = 0.29-0.74), born outside Australia (aOR = 0.71;95%CI = 0.51-0.99), higher among those reporting recent HIV PrEP use (aOR = 2.80;95%CI = 1.30-5.99), familiarity with antimicrobial resistance (aOR = 2.26;95%CI = 1.61-3.18), and willingness to take an antibiotic pill after sex to prevent STIs (aOR = 5.42;95%CI = 3.85-7.61). Willingness was high and aligned more with prevention engagement and biomedical prevention attitudes than with sexual risk behaviours, suggesting future gonorrhoea vaccines may be acceptable in this population.

title: Impact of Earthquake-Related Mass Casualty Burden on Hospital Microbial Ecology and Surgical Site Infections After Elective Orthopaedic Surgery: A Retrospective Cohort Study
abstract: The aim of this study was to compare surgical site infections (SSIs) developing after primary elective orthopaedic procedures before and after the February 6, 2023 earthquakes and to investigate the incidence, causative pathogen distribution, and antimicrobial resistance patterns. This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients undergoing primary total or partial hip arthroplasty, total knee arthroplasty, or open reduction and internal fixation. The Patients were divided into pre-earthquake (June 1, 2018-February 5, 2023) and post-earthquake (June 1, 2023-November 1, 2025) periods. The SSI cases were defined according to periprosthetic joint infection (ICM 2025) and fracture-related infection (FRI 2018) criteria. Microbiological profiles, resistance patterns, and clinical outcomes were compared between groups. A total of 99 and 118 SSI cases were identified in the pre- and post-earthquake cohorts, respectively. Overall SSI rates were similar between groups (0.98% vs. 1.19%; p=0.143). However, post-earthquake infections were associated with significantly longer hospital stays (28 vs. 22 days; p=0.025) and increased debridement procedures (2.0 vs. 1.0; p=0.006). Polymicrobial infections increased significantly (12.1% vs. 23.7%; p=0.028). A marked microbiological shift was observed, with Gram-negative organisms becoming predominant (67.7% vs. 47.6%; p=0.004), while Gram-positive organisms decreased. Staphylococcus aureus isolation significantly declined (35.4% vs. 17.2%; p=0.008). Meticillin resistance among Gram-positive isolates increased (34.9% vs. 60.0%; p=0.022), whereas no significant change in Gram-negative carbapenem resistance was observed. Our study results showed that the rates of polymicrobial infections and meticillin resistance among Gram-positive isolates increased significantly. This microbiological shift was also associated with clinically relevant outcomes, including prolonged hospital stay and an increased number of debridement procedures. Taken together, in centers exposed to a high burden of mass casualty patients, the infection dynamics of routine elective surgical cases may continue to evolve even months after the disaster. Reassessment of existing empirical treatment protocols is warranted in such settings.

title: Unexplained Colistin Resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae: Insights into sRNA-Mediated Post-Transcriptional Regulation
abstract: Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic used to treat infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens, including Klebsiella pneumoniae. Resistance to colistin can be explained by canonical mechanisms involving chromosomal mutations that activate lipid A modification pathways or by acquisition of plasmid-mediated mcr genes. These mechanisms modify the net charge of the bacterial outer membrane, reducing the binding affinity of colistin. However, an increasing number of genomic surveillance studies report colistin-resistant K. pneumoniae isolates that lack detectable alterations in known resistance mechanisms. This genotype-phenotype discordance suggests that additional regulatory mechanisms may contribute to colistin resistance. This review evaluates the hypothesis that mutation-independent regulatory changes within the PhoP/PhoQ-PmrA/PmrB-CrrA/CrrB signaling network may alter the output of lipid A modification pathways in isolates lacking detectable canonical resistance determinants. This model remains to be experimentally validated. The role of small regulatory RNAs (sRNAs) as potential post-transcriptional modulators of regulatory networks involved in envelope remodeling and antimicrobial susceptibility is explored as a potential explanation for this genotype-phenotype discordance. Finally, experimental approaches including transcriptomics, RNA-RNA interaction mapping, and functional validation are discussed as strategies to study sRNA-mediated regulatory networks. Understanding these regulatory mechanisms may help explain unresolved resistance phenotypes and refine antimicrobial resistance surveillance frameworks.

title: Central line-associated bloodstream infections outside the intensive care unit: Burden, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility identified through a Victorian surveillance program
abstract: Prevention of central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) is a priority in Australian intensive care units (ICUs). However, the epidemiology of CLABSI in non-ICU settings remains inadequately characterised, despite extensive use of central lines beyond the ICU. We aimed to determine CLABSI rates and microbiological aetiology in non-ICU wards and to compare these with corresponding ICU data from Victorian hospitals. CLABSI surveillance was undertaken voluntarily in non-ICU wards by Victorian health services between 2014 and 2025, utilising the Victorian Healthcare Associated Infection Surveillance System (VICNISS) CLABSI surveillance module, capturing CLABSI rates per 1000 central line days (CLD) as well as bloodstream infections related to mucosal barrier injury (MBI-BSI), in accordance with CDC/NHSN criteria. Retrospective analysis was performed to determine rates, pathogens, and antimicrobial susceptibility. Sixteen facilities participated in surveillance during the study period. 67 CLABSI events and 66,096 central line days were reported in non-ICU wards (predominantly haematology-oncology), corresponding to a CLABSI rate of 1.01 per 1000 CLD, which was significantly higher than the contemporaneous ICU CLABSI rate of 0.50 per 1000 CLD (IRR 3.13, 95% CI 1.88-5.22, p = 0.000). The most frequent pathogens responsible for non-ICU CLABSI were coagulase-negative Staphylococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, and Pseudomonas spp. A large burden of MBI-BSI events (n = 90) were also reported. CLABSI rates outside ICU are significantly higher than those reported in ICU settings. A substantial burden of CLABSI and MBI-BSI events were identified in haematology-oncology populations, supporting focused surveillance and infection prevention efforts in these high-risk cohorts.

title: Treatment variability among people assigned male at birth with repeat positive Mycoplasma genitalium tests: a case series
abstract: Mycoplasma genitalium (MG) can cause nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) and symptomatic proctitis. Rising antimicrobial resistance and lack of clinically available molecular resistance assays make MG treatment challenging. This study adds systematic data on the effectiveness of alternative MG regimens. Adult natal male patients who attended a public Sexual Health Clinic (SHC) and had ≥2 positive MG nucleic acid amplification tests within any 6-month period from January 2023-September 2025 were included. We classified cases as persistent infection or reinfection using clinical, demographic and self-reported behavioral data. For each patient, we summarized total number of visits, number, duration and components of each antibiotic regimen, and outcomes by MG clinical syndrome and infection status (persistence vs reinfection). Among 3,009 SHC patients, 400 (13%) had incident MG and 19 (4.8%) met inclusion criteria for repeat MG infection across 61 clinic visits. Nongonococcal urethritis (n=14/19 patients, 74%) and proctitis (n=2/19 patients, 10%) were the most prevalent syndromes. Suspected reinfection was common (40%). All 19 patients achieved cure, including 10 (53%) with microbiologic and 9 (47%) with presumed clinical cure, after treatment for a mean of 18-49 days with between 1-9 antibiotic regimens. Eight (53%) patients were cured with doxycycline plus moxifloxacin, two (100%) with doxycycline plus pristinamycin, three (75%) with minocycline alone, and three (75%) with prolonged minocycline plus tinidazole treatment. Despite frequent reinfection, most repeat positive tests represented persistent MG infections. All cases achieved cure after initial treatment failure, but many required multiple regimens over several weeks.

title: Pharmacological and Therapeutic Insights into Gepotidacin: A First-in-Class Triazaacenaphthylene Antibiotic
abstract: The growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance has necessitated the development of new antibiotics with novel mechanisms of action. Gepotidacin is a first-in-class triazaacenaphthylene antibiotic developed for the treatment of uncomplicated urinary tract infections (uUTIs) in female adults and adolescents. It inhibits bacterial DNA replication by targeting both DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV at a distinct binding site, differing from fluoroquinolones and therefore presenting a novel mechanism of action. However, resistance-associated mutations affecting susceptibility have been documented, emphasizing the need for ongoing monitoring. Pharmacokinetic studies indicate predictable, dose-dependent oral absorption suitable for twice- or thrice-daily dosing, with minimal accumulation and comparable profiles across populations. In terms of therapeutic success for the treatment of uUTIs, phase III clinical trials (EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3) have demonstrated that gepotidacin was non‑inferior to the broad-spectrum antibiotic nitrofurantoin in EAGLE-2 and even superior to nitrofurantoin in EAGLE-3, with a tolerability profile comparable to other antibiotics of its class. Studies also suggest potential efficacy against uncomplicated gonorrhea (GC), including strains resistant to current therapies. Adverse events were generally mild to moderate, predominantly gastrointestinal, and caution is advised in patients with QT prolongation risk. While gepotidacin represents an important addition to the limited pool of oral antibiotics for these infections, its long-term clinical utility will depend on careful stewardship, resistance surveillance, and further evaluation in broader indications and combination regimens.

title: Simplified bacterial identification and antimicrobial resistance detection in bacteraemia by on-chip multiplexed LAMP from blood cultures
abstract: Bacteraemia is a severe infection associated with high risks of complications and mortality. Diagnosis relies mainly on blood cultures, followed by culture-based methods, which remain the gold-standard but are time-consuming. Isothermal bacterial DNA amplification provides a rapid, reliable and cost-effective alternative for identifying and characterising bacteria directly from positive blood cultures, enabling a timelier diagnosis, particularly in resources-limited settings. However, routine implementation has been hindered by sample processing requirements and its limited multiplexing capacity. Here, we developed an on-chip loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) workflow, ALADIM (accessible and integrated LAMP analysis for multiplex detection of infectious agents in microfluidics), that integrates bacterial extraction and multiplex LAMP, followed by instrument-free amplicons detection using lateral flow immunoassay (LFIA), all within two hours (24-48 hours for the gold-standard). To demonstrate the capabilities of our device, we targeted the most common bacteria found in bacteraemia,, the co-amplification of two highly prevalent antimicrobial resistance genes,and, and the detection of a positive control. Multiplex LAMP followed by LFIA detection was first evaluated using 14 strains cultured in LB. On-chip results were comparable to those obtained with our reference method (tube-based LAMP in a thermocycler followed by LFIA detection), showing 100% sensitivity, >84% specificity for the detection ofand, and 68% sensitivity, 83% specificity for. As a proof of concept for the applicability of the complete ALADIM workflow, we analysed positive overnight blood cultures spiked with 15 strains resulting in 61 independent experiments (DNA extraction/amplification/LFA readout). In this complex matrix, ALADIM specificity remained above 77% for all targets, while sensitivity exceeded 94% forandbut decreased to 56% for. A similar decrease in overall sensitivity was observed for the in-tube method (>68%), highlighting the challenges associated with direct whole-blood analysis. This feasibility study shows the integration of multiplex DNA amplification, microfluidic processing, and LFIA detection in a single platform. Future work will focus on improving sample preparation, assay performance in complex matrices, and expanding multiplexing capabilities of ALADIM towards additional targets, to deliver a clinically reliable point-of-care testing device for low- and middle-income countries.

title: Curcumin-based nanotherapeutics for colibacillosis in chickens: advances in veterinary microbiology
abstract: One of the most important bacterial agents of colibacillosis is Avian Pathogenic Escherichia coli (APEC), which affects the poultry industry by increasing mortality, reducing growth performance, and ultimately decreasing production efficiency. According the surveillance studies carried out in the European Union during the period of 2019-21, resistance to antibiotics has increased in E. coli due to transfer of genes between bacteria and humans. The rapid emergence of high antimicrobial resistance has accelerated research towards effective, natural, and antibiotic-free substitutes. Curcumin is a bioactive polyphenol extracted from Curcuma longa, has been widely studied for its antioxidant, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory properties. But, its use as a feed additive for chickens is limited because of the low bioavailability, rapid metabolism, and poor solubility. By applying nanotechnology techniques, researchers have successfully developed formulations that counteract these disadvantages and improve their bioavailability and stability. Curcumin nanoparticles work by causing damage to bacterial cell membrane, production of reactive oxygen species, and impeding bacterial cytokinesis by preventing the assembly of the FtsZ protein. Applications of nanoformulations of curcumin as a therapeutic agent for increasing the production of chicken, the various methods of delivering them to the birds, their pharmacokinetic studies and their effect on the growth performance of poultry birds have been critically and thoroughly analyzed in this review. Nanocurcumin at a concentration of 100 mg per kilogram of feed has demonstrated the best results for body weight gain, feed conversion ratio and feed intake. Despite the positive results, there are unsolved queries about the toxicokinetics, signaling molecular pathways, long-term safety, and dose standardization. For nanocurcumin to be logically incorporated into chicken health management, these obstacles must be overcome.

title: Pharmaceutical Pollution in India: Industrial Clustering, Environmental Hotspots, Antimicrobial Resistance, and Regulatory Gaps
abstract: Pharmaceutical pollution has emerged as a critical threat to environmental integrity and public health globally, with India occupying a uniquely prominent position as both the world's leading generic drug manufacturer and a major hotspot of active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) contamination. This review synthesizes current evidence on the distribution, magnitude, and health consequences of pharmaceutical pollution across India's principal manufacturing clusters and river systems, with particular emphasis on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as a downstream public health consequence. Evidence environmental monitoring data, regulatory documentation, and case studies from Patancheru-Hyderabad (Telangana) and Baddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh (Himachal Pradesh), we highlight evidence demonstrating that active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) in pharmaceutical manufacturing hotspots frequently occur at concentrations far exceeding recommended environmental thresholds, while also documenting the occurrence of hazardous heavy metals and organic solvents in affected environments. We further assess the regulatory landscape, including the Environment (Protection) Act (1986), Biomedical Waste Management Rules (2016), Zero Liquid Discharge mandates, and recent CPCB draft guidelines (2025), and identify persistent structural gaps in monitoring, enforcement, and compound-specific discharge standards. The review concludes with evidence-based recommendations for strengthening surveillance frameworks, integrating ecological risk quotient approaches, and aligning Indian policy with emerging international standards. Addressing pharmaceutical pollution is not merely an environmental imperative but an essential component of the global effort to contain AMR, protect vulnerable populations, and achieve health sustainability in low- and middle-income countries.

Antioxidant-producing extremophile regulates gut microbiota of black soldier fly larvae to inhibit conjugative transfer mediated by plasmids in municipal sludge
abstract: Oxidative stress induced by heavy metals and antibiotics in municipal sludge inhibits the gut development of black soldier fly larvae (BSFL), compromising pollutant-processing capacity of their gut microbiota. Herein, Deinococcus radiodurans was colonized into the BSFL gut and established an antioxidant cascade regulatory system in concert with the gut microbiota, synergistically reducing the enrichment of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in municipal sludge. Results showed that bioaugmentation with Deinococcus radiodurans scavenges reactive oxygen species and upregulates the expression of G-protein and s14e genes in BSFL gut, maintaining normal gut function. On this basis, we propose two potential mechanisms responsible for inhibiting the horizontal transfer of ARGs (HGT). At the molecular level, bioaugmentation reduces environmental co-selection pressure through heavy metal immobilization mediated by extracellular polymeric substances and SlpA protein, as well as antibiotic degradation driven by gut microbiota, reducing the abundances of the class 1 integron integrase gene (intI1), conjugative transfer gene (traG), and ARGs (aphA and tetA) in municipal sludge by more than one order of magnitude. At the ecological level, bioaugmentation reshapes the microbial community structure of sludge, reducing the abundance of Pseudomonadota carrying mobile genetic elements and ARGs by approximately 26%. Moreover, bioaugmentation disrupted the co-occurrence of the mer operon and ARGs (sul1). Conjugative experiments revealed that co-cultivation with Deinococcus radiodurans reduced the conjugative transfer frequency of the ARG-carrying RP4 plasmid by 91%. Therefore, this study elucidates how antioxidant-producing extremophiles can strengthen BSFL system to inhibit HGT and reduce ARG enrichment.

Riluzole attenuates staphyloxanthin biosynthesis and biofilm formation in Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: The rapid emergence and dissemination of antibiotic resistance in Staphylococcus aureus, especially methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), pose a major global health challenge and call for alternative therapeutic strategies. S. aureus uses staphyloxanthin (STX) and biofilm as complementary virulence-associated traits that promote immune evasion and persistence at infection sites. STX protects bacteria from reactive oxygen species, while biofilms provide a structured barrier that enhances tolerance to host and antimicrobial stress. Targeting these traits may offer a non-bactericidal strategy for infection control. Here, we identified riluzole as an inhibitor of carotenoid production at non-growth-inhibitory concentrations (IC = 34.76 μg/mL) and enhances the susceptibility of S. aureus to immune cell killing. Mechanistically, riluzole interacted with CrtN (KD = 48.6 μM) and reduced its enzymatic activity, while transcriptomic analyses revealed broader transcriptional remodeling associated with reduced expression of several STX biosynthetic genes. In addition, riluzole induced membrane-associated physiological stress, including increased membrane permeability, altered membrane fluidity, ATP depletion, enhanced colistin susceptibility, and inhibition of biofilm formation. Riluzole also attenuated Pseudomonas aeruginosa-associated stimulation of S. aureus pigmentation and oxidative-stress protection. In a murine skin infection model, riluzole promoted bacterial clearance and was associated with improved wound repair. Collectively, these findings substantiate the anti-virulence properties of riluzole against S. aureus, and provide a rationale for its further development as a novel therapeutic strategy for MRSA infections.
